    65  
    66                  By the President of the United States of America
    67  
    68                  A Proclamation
    69  
    70                  1. In Proclamation 11048 of July 20, 2026 (Imposing 
    71                  Additional Duties To Offset Canadian Discrimination 
    72                  Against the Commerce of the United States With Respect 
    73                  to Motor Vehicles), I found as a fact that Canada is 
    74                  discriminating in fact against the commerce of the 
    75                  United States through Canada's motor vehicle tariff 
    76                  scheme; that this discrimination places the commerce of 
    77                  the United States at a disadvantage compared to the 
    78                  commerce of other countries; and that Canada's 
    79                  imposition is unreasonable, is not equally enforced 
    80                  upon the like articles of every foreign country, and 
    81                  places a burden on the commerce of the United States. 
    82                  To offset the burden or disadvantage on U.S. commerce 
    83                  from Canada's discrimination or unreasonable and 
    84                  unequal imposition on U.S. auto and auto parts exports, 
    85                  I imposed under section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 
    86                  (19 U.S.C. 1338) (section 338) additional ad valorem 
    87                  duties, effective August 19, 2026, on certain products 
    88                  of Canada.
    89  
    90                  2. In Proclamation 11056 of August 18, 2026 (Temporary 
    91                  Suspension of Additional Duties To Offset Canadian 
    92                  Discrimination Against the Commerce of the United 
    93                  States With Respect to Alcoholic Beverages, Dairy, and 
    94                  Motor Vehicles), I temporarily suspended for 3 days the 
    95                  effective date of the additional ad valorem duties 
    96                  imposed under Proclamation 11048 after Canada expressed 
    97                  a commitment to remove the discrimination or 
    98                  unreasonable and unequal imposition at issue in 
    99                  Proclamation 11048.
   100  
   101                  3. On August 21, 2026, Canada reneged on its 
   102                  commitment, ceased negotiating in good faith, and did 
   103                  not remove the discrimination or unreasonable and 
   104                  unequal imposition at issue in Proclamation 11048.
   105  
   106                  4. Accordingly, at 12:01 a.m. eastern time on August 
   107                  22, 2026, the 3-day suspension imposed by Proclamation 
   108                  11056 lapsed, and the additional ad valorem duties 
   109                  imposed under Proclamation 11048 became effective.
   110  
   111                  5. In Proclamation 11065 of September 8, 2026 
   112                  (Modifying the Scope of Products of Canada Subject to 
   113                  the Additional Duties Imposed To Offset Canadian 
   114                  Discrimination Against the Commerce of the United 
   115                  States With Respect to Motor Vehicles), I modified the 
   116                  duties imposed under Proclamation 11048 after receiving 
   117                  certain information, opinions, and recommendations from 
   118                  senior executive branch officials to continue 
   119                  offsetting the burden or disadvantage on U.S. commerce 
   120                  and better serve the public interest.
   121  
   122                  6. I have received certain additional information, 
   123                  opinions, and recommendations from senior executive 
   124                  branch officials on the status of the circumstances 
   125                  involved in Proclamation 11048 and the effect of the 
   126                  additional ad valorem duties imposed in Proclamation 
   127                  11048, as amended, including how effectively those 
   128                  duties are offsetting the burden or disadvantage on 
   129                  U.S. commerce. According to senior executive branch 
   130                  officials, although the additional ad valorem duties 
   131                  imposed in Proclamation 11048, as amended, offset the 
   132                  burden or disadvantage on U.S. commerce, modifying the 
   133                  scope of products
   134  
   135  [[Page 68862]]
   136  
   137                  subject to the additional ad valorem duties imposed in 
   138                  Proclamation 11048, as amended, would still offset the 
   139                  burden or disadvantage on U.S. commerce and better 
   140                  serve the public interest. In my senior executive 
   141                  branch officials' opinion, modifying the scope of 
   142                  products subject to the additional ad valorem duties 
   143                  imposed in Proclamation 11048, as amended, is required 
   144                  by the public interests and is consistent with the 
   145                  interests of the United States.
   146  
   147                  7. After considering the information, opinions, and 
   148                  recommendations that have been provided to me by senior 
   149                  executive branch officials, among other relevant 
   150                  information and considerations, I determine that the 
   151                  public interests require modifying the scope of 
   152                  products subject to the additional ad valorem duties 
   153                  imposed in Proclamation 11048, as amended.
   154  
   155                  8. In my judgment, the modification in this 
   156                  proclamation will offset the burden or disadvantage on 
   157                  U.S. commerce, is consistent with the public interests 
   158                  and the interests of the United States, is required by 
   159                  the public interests, and will better serve the public 
   160                  interest.
   161  
   162                  9. Section 338 authorizes the President, if he 
   163                  determines it will serve the public interest, to offset 
   164                  any burden or disadvantage placed on the commerce of 
   165                  the United States by an unequal imposition or 
   166                  discrimination by a foreign country by specifying and 
   167                  declaring additional duties not to exceed 50 percent ad 
   168                  valorem (or its equivalent) and not to take effect 
   169                  earlier than 30 days after the President's proclamation 
   170                  finding that a foreign country is imposing an 
   171                  unreasonable charge, exaction, regulation, or 
   172                  limitation that is not equally enforced on the like 
   173                  articles of every foreign country, or discriminates in 
   174                  fact against U.S. commerce in a way that places the 
   175                  commerce of the United States at a disadvantage 
   176                  compared to the commerce of any foreign country. 
   177                  Section 338 also authorizes the President to suspend, 
   178                  revoke, supplement, or amend any proclamation under 
   179                  section 338 whenever the President deems that the 
   180                  public interests require such action. Further, section 
   181                  338 authorizes the President to exclude from 
   182                  importation articles of the foreign country if the 
   183                  foreign country maintains or increases the 
   184                  discrimination against the commerce of the United 
   185                  States and the President deems the exclusion to be 
   186                  consistent with the public interests and the interests 
   187                  of the United States.
   188  
   189                  10. Section 604 of the Trade Act of 1974, as amended 
   190                  (19 U.S.C. 2483) (section 604), authorizes the 
   191                  President to embody in the Harmonized Tariff Schedule 
   192                  of the United States (HTSUS) the substance of statutes 
   193                  affecting import treatment, and actions thereunder, 
   194                  including the removal, modification, continuance, or 
   195                  imposition of any rate of duty or other import 
   196                  restriction.
   197  
   198                  NOW, THEREFORE, I, DONALD J. TRUMP, President of the 
   199                  United States of America, by the authority vested in me 
   200                  by the Constitution and the laws of the United States, 
   201                  including section 338; section 301 of title 3, United 
   202                  States Code; and section 604, do hereby proclaim as 
   203                  follows:
   204  
   205                      (1) Except as otherwise provided in this 
   206                  proclamation, certain products of Canada, as set forth 
   207                  in Annex I, Part A to this proclamation, imported into 
   208                  the United States shall no longer be subject to the 
   209                  additional ad valorem duty of 50 percent imposed 
   210                  pursuant to Proclamation 11048, as amended. In 
   211                  addition, certain products of Canada, as set forth in 
   212                  Annex I, Part B to this proclamation, imported into the 
   213                  United States shall be subject to the additional ad 
   214                  valorem duty of 50 percent imposed pursuant to 
   215                  Proclamation 11048, as amended. The duties imposed 
   216                  pursuant to Proclamation 11048, as amended, and as 
   217                  modified in this proclamation, shall apply in addition 
   218                  to duties imposed pursuant to section 232 of the Trade 
   219                  Expansion Act of 1962, as amended (19 U.S.C. 1862). 
   220                  These changes shall be effective with respect to goods 
   221                  entered for consumption, or withdrawn from warehouse 
   222                  for consumption, on or after 12:01 a.m. eastern time on 
   223                  October 30, 2026.
   224                      (2) The HTSUS is modified as provided in Annex II 
   225                  to this proclamation, effective with respect to goods 
   226                  entered for consumption, or withdrawn from warehouse 
   227                  for consumption, on or after 12:01 a.m. eastern time on 
   228                  October 30, 2026, and the modifications shall continue 
   229                  in effect unless this action is expressly suspended, 
   230                  revoked, supplemented, amended, or terminated.
   231  
   232  [[Page 68863]]
   233  
   234                      (3) The head of each executive department and 
   235                  agency (agency) is authorized to and shall take all 
   236                  appropriate measures within the agency's authority to 
   237                  implement this proclamation. The head of each agency 
   238                  may, consistent with applicable law, including section 
   239                  301 of title 3, United States Code, redelegate the 
   240                  authority to take such appropriate measures within the 
   241                  agency.
   242                      (4) The Commissioner of U.S. Customs and Border 
   243                  Protection (CBP), in consultation with the Secretary of 
   244                  the Treasury, the Secretary of Commerce, and the United 
   245                  States Trade Representative, is authorized to issue 
   246                  such rules, regulations, guidance, instructions, or 
   247                  determinations as may be necessary to implement this 
   248                  proclamation and is authorized to take any necessary 
   249                  measures to administer this proclamation.
   250                      (5) The Commissioner of CBP, in consultation with 
   251                  the Secretary of the Treasury, the Secretary of 
   252                  Commerce, the United States Trade Representative, the 
   253                  Chairman of the United States International Trade 
   254                  Commission, and any other senior executive branch 
   255                  official the Commissioner of CBP deems appropriate, 
   256                  shall determine whether any additional modifications to 
   257                  the HTSUS are necessary to effectuate this proclamation 
   258                  and shall make such modifications to the HTSUS through 
   259                  notice in the Federal Register, including any technical 
   260                  or ministerial correction to the annexes to this 
   261                  proclamation.
   262                      (6) For any rule or regulation the Commissioner of 
   263                  CBP makes to implement this proclamation, the 
   264                  Commissioner of CBP shall, to the extent required by 
   265                  law, obtain the approval of the President or the United 
   266                  States Trade Representative. The United States Trade 
   267                  Representative is delegated the President's approval 
   268                  authority in 19 U.S.C. 1338(h).
   269                      (7) Any provision of previous proclamations and 
   270                  Executive Orders that is inconsistent with this 
   271                  proclamation is superseded to the extent of such 
   272                  inconsistency.
   273                      (8) If any provision of this proclamation or the 
   274                  application of any provision to any individual or 
   275                  circumstance is held to be invalid, the remainder of 
   276                  this proclamation and the application of its provisions 
   277                  to any other individuals or circumstances shall not be 
   278                  affected.
   279

    64  Notice of Actions in Section 301 Investigations of Acts, 
    65  Policies, and Practices of Various Economies Related to the Failure of 
    66  Each Economy To Impose and Effectively Enforce a Prohibition on the 
    67  Importation of Goods Produced With Forced Labor
    68  
    69  AGENCY: Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR).
    70  
    71  ACTION: Notice of action.
    72  
    73  -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    74  
    75  SUMMARY: The United States Trade Representative (Trade Representative) 
    76  has determined under Section 301(b) and Section 304(a) of the Trade Act 
    77  of 1974, as amended (Trade Act), that in each of 60 investigations, 
    78  certain of the acts, policies, and practices of the economy at issue 
    79  are actionable and that action by the United States is appropriate. In 
    80  accordance with the specific direction of the President, the Trade 
    81  Representative is taking actions in each of these investigations by 
    82  imposing tariffs on all products of the investigated economy, with 
    83  certain exemptions as provided in Annexes I and II to this notice 
    84  (Notice). Consistent with the specific direction of the President, for 
    85  an economy that imposes a forced labor import prohibition, has 
    86  committed to impose and enforce such a prohibition through an Agreement 
    87  on Reciprocal Trade (ART), or has imposed a partial regime with the 
    88  effect of preventing the importation of certain forced labor goods, the 
    89  Trade Representative has determined 10 percent is the appropriate rate 
    90  of Section 301 duties, with specific economies subject to a 10 percent 
    91  rate net of a product's most-favored-nation (MFN) duty. For every other 
    92  economy, and in accordance with the specific direction of the 
    93  President, the Trade Representative has determined 12.5 percent is the 
    94  appropriate rate of Section 301 duty, with specific economies subject 
    95  to a 12.5 percent rate net of a product's MFN duty. The Trade 
    96  Representative has also determined, consistent with the specific 
    97  direction of the President, to establish, when feasible, tariff-rate 
    98  quotas (TRQs) for Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, and Malaysia, based 
    99  on each economy's importation of U.S. inputs, to encourage the 
   100  importation by each of these economies of U.S. cotton and textile 
   101  goods, in order to reduce reliance on inputs from other sources that 
   102  are more likely to contain forced labor inputs.
   103  
   104  DATES: The additional rates of duty are applicable with respect to 
   105  products that are entered for consumption, or withdrawn from warehouse 
   106  for consumption, on or after 12:01 a.m. eastern time on July 24, 2026, 
   107  except that goods loaded onto a vessel at the port of loading and in 
   108  transit on the final mode of transit before 12:01 a.m. eastern time on 
   109  July 24, 2026, and entered for consumption or withdrawn from warehouse 
   110  for consumption before 12:01 a.m. eastern time on July 28, 2026, shall 
   111  not be subject to such additional duty.
   112  
   113  FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT: For general questions about this 
   114  Notice, contact Megan Grimball and Philip Butler, Chairs of the Section 
   115  301 Committee, at (202) 395-5725.
   116  
   117  SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
   118  
   119  I. Proceedings in the Investigations
   120  
   121      On March 12, 2026, the Trade Representative initiated 60 
   122  investigations related to the failure of various economies to each 
   123  impose and effectively enforce a prohibition on the importation of 
   124  goods produced wholly or in part with forced labor (forced labor import 
   125  prohibition), pursuant to 302(b)(1) of the Trade Act (19 U.S.C. 
   126  2412(b)(1)). See 91 FR 12884 (published March 17, 2026).
   127      On June 2, 2026, the Trade Representative determined that, in each 
   128  of the 60 investigations, certain of the acts, polices, and practices 
   129  of the economy at issue are actionable under sections 301(b) and 304(a) 
   130  of the Trade Act. The Trade Representative also issued a comprehensive 
   131  report, Acts, Policies, and Practices of Various Economies Related to 
   132  the Failure to Impose and Effectively Enforce a Prohibition on the 
   133  Importation of Goods Produced with Forced Labor (Report). Specifically, 
   134  the Trade Representative determined that:
   135       The following 54 economies have failed to impose and 
   136  effectively enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods produced 
   137  with forced labor: Algeria; Angola; Argentina; Australia; the Bahamas; 
   138  Bahrain; Bangladesh; Brazil; Cambodia; Chile; China, People's Republic 
   139  of; Colombia; Costa Rica; Dominican Republic; Egypt; El Salvador; 
   140  Guatemala; Guyana; Honduras; Hong Kong, China; India; Iraq; Israel; 
   141  Japan; Jordan; Kazakhstan; Kuwait; Libya; Malaysia; Morocco; New 
   142  Zealand; Nicaragua; Nigeria; Norway; Oman; Peru; the Philippines; 
   143  Qatar; Russia; Saudi Arabia; Singapore; South Africa; South Korea; Sri 
   144  Lanka; Switzerland; Taiwan; Thailand; Trinidad and Tobago; 
   145  T[uuml]rkiye; United Arab Emirates; United Kingdom; Uruguay; Venezuela; 
   146  and Vietnam.
   147       The following six economies have failed to effectively 
   148  enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods produced with forced 
   149  labor: Canada, Ecuador, the European Union, Indonesia, Mexico, and 
   150  Pakistan.
   151       All of the investigated economies have failed to impose a 
   152  forced labor import prohibition and to effectively enforce such a 
   153  prohibition (that is to say, all of the economies have failed to 
   154  satisfy both factors in these investigations).
   155      The Trade Representative proposed to determine that action is 
   156  appropriate in each investigation, and that appropriate action would 
   157  include tariffs on all products of an economy, with certain exemptions. 
   158  The Trade Representative also proposed a textile mechanism that would 
   159  allow for a certain volume of apparel and textile imports from certain 
   160  economies to enter the United States at a reduced Section 301 tariff 
   161  rate. See 91 FR 34272 (published June 5, 2026) (the June 5, 2026 FRN).
   162      The June 5, 2026 FRN invited public comments on the proposed 
   163  actions to be taken in each investigation. The June 5, 2026 FRN 
   164  proposed applying tariffs of 10 percent for each economy that imposes a 
   165  forced labor import prohibition; has taken on commitments related to 
   166  forced labor import prohibitions through an ART; or has imposed a 
   167  partial regime with the effect of preventing the importation of certain 
   168  forced labor goods. The June 5, 2026 FRN proposed applying tariffs of 
   169  12.5 percent for every other economy. The tariff proposals in each 
   170  investigation included exemptions for certain goods, including 
   171  informational materials, donations, accompanied baggage, all articles 
   172  and parts of articles subject to tariffs under Section 232 of the Trade 
   173  Expansion Act of 1962, and certain products identified in Annex A to 
   174  the June 5, 2026 FRN.
   175      As explained in the June 5, 2026 FRN, the proposed exemptions 
   176  included: (a) raw materials that, if subject to the proposed additional 
   177  tariffs, could lead to the unavailability of domestic supply; (b) 
   178  products that could cause economy-wide disruptions if subject to 
   179  additional tariffs; (c) certain products that cannot be grown or 
   180  produced in sufficient quantities in the United States or obtained from 
   181  other sources; and (d) articles for which additional tariffs may not 
   182  contribute substantially to the elimination of the acts, policies, and 
   183  practices determined to be actionable in the investigations.
   184      Interested persons were invited to provide comments regarding the 
   185  scope
   186  
   187  [[Page 47319]]
   188  
   189  of tariff coverage (including the proposed excluded products identified 
   190  in Annex A to the June 5, 2026 FRN and the proposed textile mechanism. 
   191  With respect to the tariff proposals, the June 5, 2026 FRN stated that, 
   192  in considering whether certain articles should be subject to additional 
   193  duties under Section 301 of the Trade Act, USTR will consider the needs 
   194  of the U.S. economy. With respect to comments on the inclusion or 
   195  removal of particular tariff subheadings subject to the proposed 
   196  action, USTR requested that comments address specifically whether the 
   197  products under the tariff subheading are necessary raw materials that 
   198  if subject to the proposed tariff could lead to the unavailability of 
   199  domestic supply; whether additional tariffs would cause serious 
   200  dislocations in the supply of the products and could cause economy-wide 
   201  disruptions, or other similar factors; and whether imposing additional 
   202  tariffs on products under the tariff subheading would be practicable or 
   203  effective in obtaining the elimination of the investigated acts, 
   204  policies, and practices.
   205      USTR also requested public comments regarding the proposed actions, 
   206  including whether the products in Annex A to the June 5, 2026 FRN were 
   207  appropriately excluded; the level of the increase, if any, in the rate 
   208  of duty; whether differential tariff rates should be applied to an 
   209  economy where the economy has made a commitment to the United States to 
   210  impose and enforce a forced labor import prohibition, has imposed a 
   211  forced labor import prohibition, or has imposed a partial regime with 
   212  the effect of preventing the importation of certain forced labor goods; 
   213  and features of the proposed textile mechanism, including the U.S. and 
   214  foreign products to be covered, the relative market opportunities for 
   215  each side, and the tariff rate (if any) to be applied to products 
   216  subject to the mechanism, as well as whether a similar mechanism should 
   217  apply to any other product or sector.
   218      In response to the June 5, 2026 FRN, USTR received over 1,600 
   219  written comments. USTR and the Section 301 Committee held a three-day 
   220  public hearing on July 7, 8, and 9, 2026, regarding the proposed 
   221  actions. During the hearings, over 100 witnesses provided testimony and 
   222  responded to questions. Witnesses included representatives of the 
   223  governments of certain investigated economies, industry associations, 
   224  domestic producers, and non-governmental organizations. The public 
   225  submissions are available at: https://comments.ustr.gov/s/ at docket 
   226  numbers USTR-2026-0265 and USTR-2026-0266. Transcripts of the hearings 
   227  are available on USTR's website.
   228      Following government-to-government consultations pursuant to 
   229  Section 303 of the Trade Act and the publication of proposed actions in 
   230  the June 5, 2026 FRN, additional economies have imposed forced labor 
   231  import prohibitions--Cambodia, Guatemala, Honduras, India, Sri Lanka, 
   232  and Trinidad and Tobago; or undertaken commitments regarding forced 
   233  labor import prohibitions in an ART--Jordan.
   234  
   235  II. Determinations of Action
   236  
   237  A. Overview of Responsive Actions in the Investigations
   238  
   239      On June 2, 2026, the Trade Representative determined that, in each 
   240  of the 60 investigations, certain acts, policies, and practices of the 
   241  economy at issue are unreasonable and burden or restrict U.S. commerce, 
   242  and are thus actionable under Section 301(b) of the Trade Act. Section 
   243  301(b) provides that upon determining that the acts, policies, and 
   244  practices under investigation are actionable and that action is 
   245  appropriate, the Trade Representative shall take all appropriate and 
   246  feasible action authorized under Section 301(c), subject to the 
   247  specific direction, if any, of the President regarding such action, and 
   248  all other appropriate and feasible action within the power of the 
   249  President that the President may direct the Trade Representative to 
   250  take under Section 301(b), to obtain the elimination of that act, 
   251  policy, or practice. Section 301(b) provides further that actions 
   252  ``within the power of the President'' may include ``[a]ctions . . . 
   253  with respect to trade in any goods or services, or with respect to any 
   254  other area of pertinent relations with the foreign country.''
   255      Section 301(c) of the Trade Act authorizes the Trade Representative 
   256  to take certain, specific actions for purposes of carrying out the 
   257  provisions of Section 301(b). For example, Section 301(c)(1)(B) 
   258  authorizes the Trade Representative to ``impose duties or other import 
   259  restrictions on the goods'' of the foreign country subject to the 
   260  investigation. Section 301(c)(3)(A) provides that actions that the 
   261  Trade Representative is authorized to take may be taken against any 
   262  goods or economic sector on a non-discriminatory basis or solely 
   263  against the foreign country concerned. Section 301(c)(3)(B) empowers 
   264  the Trade Representative to take actions against any goods and economic 
   265  sector ``without regard to whether or not such goods or economic sector 
   266  were involved in the act, policy, or practice that is the subject of 
   267  such action.''
   268      USTR and the Section 301 Committee have carefully reviewed the 
   269  public comments and testimony regarding the proposed actions to be 
   270  taken in each investigation. The Trade Representative informed the 
   271  President of his recommended responsive actions in each investigation, 
   272  including, for each economy, whether to impose 10 or 12.5 percent 
   273  tariffs on all products of that economy or, in the case of specific 
   274  economies, 10 or 12.5 percent tariffs net of a product's MFN duty, with 
   275  exemptions for certain goods. The Trade Representative also informed 
   276  the President of economies that have imposed forced labor import 
   277  prohibitions, or undertaken commitments regarding forced labor import 
   278  prohibitions through an ART, since June 5, 2026. The Trade 
   279  Representative also advised the President that, after considering 
   280  significant comments and testimony on the proposed actions, certain 
   281  products warranted exemption from the tariffs imposed in the 
   282  investigations as they are: (a) raw materials that if subject to these 
   283  tariffs could lead to the unavailability of domestic supply; (b) 
   284  products that could cause economy-wide disruptions if subject to these 
   285  tariffs; (c) products that cannot be grown or produced in sufficient 
   286  quantities or at reasonable prices in the United States or obtained 
   287  from other sources; (d) products for which these tariffs may not be 
   288  effective in obtaining the elimination of the acts, policies, and 
   289  practices of economies found to be actionable in the investigations; or 
   290  (e) certain products of Argentina, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Ecuador, El 
   291  Salvador, the European Union, Guatemala, Indonesia, Jordan, Malaysia, 
   292  Switzerland, Taiwan, or the United Kingdom that would encourage these 
   293  economies to fulfill commitments regarding forced labor import 
   294  prohibitions or to encourage these economies to enact and effectively 
   295  enforce a forced labor import prohibition.
   296      On July 23, 2026--after considering and taking account of the 
   297  information and advice provided by the Trade Representative; the 
   298  information, findings, and determinations in the June 5, 2026 FRN; the 
   299  need to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices of 
   300  the investigated economies found to be actionable; and other pertinent 
   301  information--the President issued a memorandum (Memorandum) directing 
   302  that:
   303  
   304      Section 1. Tariffs and Exemptions. (a) Except as otherwise 
   305  provided in this memorandum, the Trade Representative shall impose 
   306  the following tariff rates on all goods of the economy for which an 
   307  act, policy, or
   308  
   309  [[Page 47320]]
   310  
   311  practice was found actionable under section 301:
   312      (i) 10 percent tariff rate: The Trade Representative shall 
   313  impose a tariff of 10 percent on goods of Argentina, Bangladesh, 
   314  Cambodia, Canada, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, India, 
   315  Indonesia, Jordan, Malaysia, Mexico, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, the United 
   316  Kingdom, and Trinidad and Tobago.
   317      (ii) Tariff rate of 10 percent or 12.5 percent, net of MFN rate: 
   318  For a product of the European Union or Taiwan, where such product's 
   319  MFN tariff is less than 10 percent, the Trade Representative shall 
   320  impose a section 301 tariff pursuant to these investigations so that 
   321  the sum of the MFN tariff and the section 301 tariff shall be 10 
   322  percent, and where such product's MFN tariff is greater than or 
   323  equal to 10 percent, the Trade Representative shall impose a section 
   324  301 tariff of zero. For a product of Japan, Korea, or Switzerland, 
   325  where such product's MFN tariff is less than 12.5 percent, the Trade 
   326  Representative shall impose a section 301 tariff pursuant to these 
   327  investigations so that the sum of the MFN tariff and the tariff 
   328  imposed pursuant to these investigations shall be 12.5 percent, and 
   329  where such product's MFN tariff is greater than or equal to 12.5 
   330  percent, the Trade Representative shall impose a section 301 tariff 
   331  of zero. Capping total duties in this manner is feasible, consistent 
   332  with the terms of the Agreements on Reciprocal Trade or similar 
   333  arrangements, and appropriate to encourage these economies to 
   334  fulfill commitments regarding forced labor import prohibitions or to 
   335  enact and effectively enforce such a prohibition.
   336      (iii) 12.5 percent tariff rate: For goods of all other 
   337  investigated economies, the Trade Representative shall impose a 
   338  tariff rate of 12.5 percent.
   339      (b) The Trade Representative shall exempt from the tariffs 
   340  imposed as directed in subsection (a) of this section the products 
   341  identified in the Annex to this memorandum for each economy for 
   342  which an act, policy, or practice was found actionable under section 
   343  301, as the products identified constitute:
   344      (i) raw materials that if subject to these tariffs could lead to 
   345  the unavailability of domestic supply;
   346      (ii) products that could cause economy-wide disruptions if 
   347  subject to these tariffs;
   348      (iii) products that cannot be grown or produced in sufficient 
   349  quantities in the United States or obtained from other sources;
   350      (iv) products for which these tariffs may not be effective in 
   351  obtaining the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices of 
   352  economies found to be actionable in the investigations; or
   353      (v) certain products of Argentina, Bangladesh, Cambodia, 
   354  Ecuador, El Salvador, the European Union, Guatemala, Indonesia, 
   355  Jordan, Malaysia, Switzerland, Taiwan, or the United Kingdom that 
   356  would encourage these economies to fulfill commitments regarding 
   357  forced labor import prohibitions or to encourage these economies to 
   358  enact and effectively enforce a forced labor import prohibition.
   359      (c) After considering the relevant issues and factors and 
   360  weighing the relevant considerations, including potential economic 
   361  harm and efficacy of tariffs, I determine that the products 
   362  identified in the Annex to this memorandum shall be exempted from 
   363  the tariffs directed in subsection (a) of this section, and the 
   364  Trade Representative shall direct that the Harmonized Tariff 
   365  Schedule of the United States (HTSUS) be modified as provided in the 
   366  Annex to this memorandum. In my judgment, the tariffs directed in 
   367  subsection (a) of this section with the exemptions described in 
   368  subsection (b) of this section are appropriate and feasible to 
   369  obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, or practices of the 
   370  economies found to be actionable under section 301.
   371      Sec. 2. Tariff-Rate Quotas. (a) As soon as the Trade 
   372  Representative determines that it is feasible, the Trade 
   373  Representative shall:
   374      (i) establish TRQs for Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, and 
   375  Malaysia, with an initial duration of 3 years, to encourage the 
   376  importation by each of these economies of U.S. textile goods, in

   382  enter the United States free of the section 301 tariffs provided for

   384      (b) As soon as the Trade Representative determines that it is

  2095  IV. Severability of Tariff Actions
  2096  
  2097      For convenience and concision, this Notice has set out the actions 
  2098  of the Trade Representative in each of the 60 investigations of the 
  2099  acts, policies, and practices of each investigated economy related to 
  2100  its failure to enact and effectively enforce a forced labor import 
  2101  prohibition.
  2102      The actions taken by the Trade Representative in this Notice with 
  2103  respect to the acts, policies, and practices of an economy in one 
  2104  investigation are separate from the actions taken with respect to the 
  2105  acts, policies, and practices of each other economy in other 
  2106  investigations by the Trade Representative. Each tariff action as to an 
  2107  economy in one investigation is separate from every other tariff action 
  2108  in other investigations and is for the distinct purpose of obtaining 
  2109  the elimination of the applicable economy's acts, policies, and 
  2110  practices found actionable under Section 301 in that investigation.
  2111      Each tariff action on an economy taken by the Trade Representative 
  2112  in this Notice in one investigation is only for the purpose of 
  2113  obtaining the elimination of the applicable economy's acts, policies, 
  2114  and practices found actionable under Section 301 in that investigation 
  2115  and not for any other purpose.
  2116      Each tariff action as to an economy taken by the Trade 
  2117  Representative in this Notice is intended to operate independently of 
  2118  each other, and the potential invalidity of one tariff action taken in 
  2119  this Notice should not affect any other tariff. The potential 
  2120  invalidity of one aspect of any tariff action taken in this Notice 
  2121  should not affect any other aspect of the tariff action.
  2122      Should a court hold that the implementation of any tariff action 
  2123  taken by the Trade Representative in this Notice with respect to any 
  2124  Section 301 investigation to be invalid, only that tariff in that 
  2125  investigation should be treated as invalid, and any other tariff action 
  2126  taken in this Notice with respect to that investigation, or any other 
  2127  investigation, and the remainder of the actions in this Notice should 
  2128  continue to apply and should not be affected. Should a court hold that 
  2129  any aspect of any tariff action taken by the Trade Representative in 
  2130  this Notice with respect to any Section 301 investigation to be 
  2131  invalid, only that aspect of that tariff action should be treated as 
  2132  invalid.
  2133      In the Trade Representative's judgment, each tariff action taken in 
  2134  this Notice is feasible and appropriate to obtain the elimination of 
  2135  the applicable economy's acts, policies, and practices the Trade 
  2136  Representative has found actionable under Section 301 in that 
  2137  investigation. If any aspect of the tariff action for an economy is 
  2138  held to be invalid, the remaining aspects of the tariff action and each 
  2139  tariff for a product of an investigated economy would remain 
  2140  appropriate and feasible to obtain the elimination of the applicable 
  2141  economy's acts, policies, or practices found actionable under Section 
  2142  301 in that investigation.
  2143      This section reflects the Trade Representative's intent that each 
  2144  tariff action and each exemption for a product of an investigated 
  2145  economy as set forth in section II.B of this Notice remain operative to 
  2146  the maximum extent consistent with law. If any exemption to any tariff 
  2147  action taken in this Notice with respect to an investigation is held to 
  2148  be invalid in whole or in part, only that exemption or that part of the 
  2149  exemption should be treated as invalid, and no other exemption, part of 
  2150  an exemption, or application of an exemption should be treated as 
  2151  invalid. The applicable tariff action taken in this Notice would apply 
  2152  to imports of a product from the applicable economy to which the 
  2153  invalidated exemption or the invalidated part of the exemption applied 
  2154  before its invalidation.
  2155      For greater certainty, the Trade Representative has determined that 
  2156  every tariff action and exemption in each investigation as set forth in 
  2157  this Notice is lawful. This section reflects the Trade Representative's 
  2158  view that each tariff action taken by the Trade Representative in this 
  2159  Notice should remain operative to obtain the elimination of the 
  2160  applicable economy's acts, policies, and practices found actionable 
  2161  under Section 301.
  2162      The determinations in this section are consistent with the 
  2163  President's specific direction in the Memorandum that ``[e]ach tariff 
  2164  action directed in this memorandum is separate from every other and 
  2165  imposed for the distinct purpose of obtaining the elimination of the 
  2166  specific economy's act, policy, or practice found actionable under 
  2167  section 301''; that ``[e]ach tariff action directed in this memorandum, 
  2168  when implemented, is intended to operate independent of each other, and 
  2169  the potential invalidity of one tariff directed in this memorandum that 
  2170  is implemented should not affect any other tariff directed in this 
  2171  memorandum that is implemented''; that ``each tariff directed in this 
  2172  memorandum that is implemented--with any combinations of exemptions or 
  2173  even without any exemptions--should remain operative to obtain the 
  2174  elimination of the specific economy's act, policy, or practice found 
  2175  actionable under section 301''; and that ``[i]f any exemption to any 
  2176  tariff, when implemented, is held to be invalid in whole or in part, 
  2177  only that exemption or that part of the exemption should be treated 
  2178  invalid'' and ``[t]he applicable tariff action directed in this 
  2179  memorandum should apply to imports to which the invalidated exemption 
  2180  or the invalidated part of the exemption applied before its 
  2181  invalidation.'' Further, this Notice, including this section, is 
  2182  consistent with the President's directive that ``[e]ach tariff action 
  2183  directed in this memorandum is only for the purpose of obtaining the 
  2184  elimination of the specific economy's act, policy, or practice found 
  2185  actionable under section 301 and not for any other purpose.''

tools.name: fr_search

query.description: Full-text search terms; "" for none. Supports quoted phrases, e.g. "\"extension of stay\" F-1".
query.title: Query

doc_type.description: Document types: RULE, PRORULE (proposed rule), NOTICE, PRESDOCU (presidential document). null for all.
doc_type.title: Doc Type

agency.description: Agency slugs, e.g. homeland-security-department, u-s-citizenship-and-immigration-services, u-s-immigration-and-customs-enforcement, state-department, labor-department, executive-office-of-the-president.
agency.title: Agency

pres_type.description: Presidential document subtypes (use with doc_type PRESDOCU).
pres_type.title: Pres Type

cfr.description: CFR title:part affected, e.g. 8:214. The part must be numeric; lettered parts are not supported by this filter.
cfr.title: Cfr

tools.description: Search U.S. Federal Register documents (rules, proposed rules, notices, presidential documents) by keywords and filters. Prints document numbers, titles, types, dates, citations, dockets, RINs and abstracts.

tools.name: fr_doc
tools.description: Metadata for one Federal Register document: title, type, action, citation, page range, publication/signing/effective dates, comment deadline, docket, RIN, CFR parts affected, corrections, abstract.

tools.name: fr_toc
tools.description: Outline of a document's full text: headings with line numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_grep

pattern.description: Python regular expression, searched over the whole text (a match may span lines). ^ and $ match at line boundaries; . does not match a newline.
pattern.title: Pattern

context.description: Lines of context around each match (default 2, at most 10).
context.title: Context

tools.description: Regex search inside one document's full text. Shows the lines of each match with line numbers, context lines and the FR page of each match. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_text
tools.description: Read a document's full text by line range, with line numbers. [[Page N]] markers give FR page numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

answer.description: Direct answer to each lettered part, in order, labelled (a), (b), ...
answer.title: Answer

basis.description: Provisions and documents relied on, with citations.
basis.title: Basis

uncertainty.description: What the documents leave open, or "None".
uncertainty.title: Uncertainty

   286  IV. Proposed Actions To Be Taken in the Investigations
   287  
   288      Section 301(b) of the Trade Act provides that upon determining that 
   289  the acts, policies, and practices under investigation are actionable 
   290  and that action is appropriate, the Trade Representative shall take all 
   291  appropriate and feasible action authorized under section 301(c), 
   292  subject to the specific direction, if any, of the President regarding 
   293  such action, and all other appropriate and feasible action within the 
   294  power of the President, that the President may direct the Trade 
   295  Representative to take under section 301(b), to obtain the elimination 
   296  of that act, policy, or practice.
   297      Section 301(c) of the Trade Act authorizes the Trade Representative 
   298  to take certain actions for purposes of carrying out the provisions of 
   299  Section 301(b). Among others, Section 301(c)(1)(B) authorizes the Trade 
   300  Representative to ``impose duties or other import restrictions'' on the 
   301  goods of the foreign country subject to the investigation.
   302      Pursuant to Sections 301(b) and (c), the Trade Representative 
   303  proposes to determine that action is appropriate and that appropriate 
   304  action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices 
   305  would include the imposition of ad valorem duties on all products of 
   306  the 60 economies subject to investigations, except as provided in Annex 
   307  A to this Notice. The proposed exemptions in Annex A include all 
   308  articles and parts currently subject to section 232 tariffs and raw 
   309  materials that if subject to the proposed additional tariffs could lead 
   310  to the unavailability of domestic supply. Annex A also includes 
   311  products that could cause economy-wide disruptions if subject to the 
   312  proposed additional tariffs and certain products that cannot be grown 
   313  or produced in sufficient quantities in the United States or obtained 
   314  from other sources. The proposed exemptions include informational 
   315  materials (e.g., books), donations, and accompanied baggage. Finally, 
   316  the proposed exemptions include articles for which additional tariffs 
   317  may not contribute substantially to the elimination of the investigated 
   318  acts, policies, and practices described above.
   319      For economies that impose a forced labor import prohibition--
   320  Canada, Ecuador, the European Union, Indonesia, Mexico, and Pakistan; 
   321  for economies that have undertaken commitments in their respective 
   322  Agreements on Reciprocal Trade regarding forced labor import 
   323  prohibitions--Argentina, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Ecuador, El Salvador, 
   324  Guatemala, Indonesia, Malaysia, and Taiwan; and economies that have 
   325  imposed a partial regime with the effect of preventing the importation 
   326  of certain forced labor goods--the United Kingdom; the Trade 
   327  Representative proposes additional duties of 10% for products of these 
   328  economies. For all other economies that have failed to impose and 
   329  effectively enforce a forced labor import prohibition, the Trade 
   330  Representative proposes 12.5% as the rate of additional duties.
   331      The Trade Representative also proposes a textile mechanism that 
   332  would allow for a certain volume of apparel and textile imports to 
   333  enter the United States at a reduced Section 301 tariff rate. Under 
   334  such a textile mechanism, the volume of reduced-duty imports from 
   335  certain trading partners would be equivalent to the quantity of exports 
   336  of textiles (e.g., U.S. produced man-made and cotton fiber textile 
   337  inputs) from the United States to that trading partner. A certain 
   338  volume of apparel and textile imports would also be allowed to enter 
   339  the United States at the reduced Section 301 rate based on the volume 
   340  of U.S. cotton and cotton products a trading partner imports from the 
   341  United States during a certain period of time.
   342  
   343  V. Response to Significant Comments
   344  
   345      USTR responds below to significant issues raised in the public 
   346  comments and hearings in response to the March 17, 2026, Federal 
   347  Register notice.
   348  
   349  Response to Significant Comments Raising Legal Arguments Regarding 
   350  Findings of ``Unreasonableness''
   351  
   352      Multiple comments raised threshold arguments that the Trade 
   353  Representative should not find that the failure of an economy to impose 
   354  and effectively enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods 
   355  produced with forced labor is unreasonable where: (1) an economy has 
   356  domestic laws prohibiting forced labor; (2) where no international 
   357  standards exists which provide an affirmative obligation on economies 
   358  to impose a forced labor import prohibition; or (3) where an economy 
   359  has otherwise made commitments to the United States with respect to 
   360  imposing and/or enforcing a forced labor import prohibition. This 
   361  section takes each of these arguments in turn.
   362      With respect to the first argument, and as explained in the Report 
   363  and above, solely prohibiting forced labor domestically is unreasonable 
   364  because it fails to discipline the influx of forced labor goods or to 
   365  prevent domestic producers from using forced labor inputs. Thus, while 
   366  an economy may have taken steps to ensure that the condition of forced 
   367  labor is extinguished within its borders, the economy nevertheless 
   368  permits market conditions where imported forced labor goods have a 
   369  competitive advantage over U.S. goods imported into their economy.
   370      In response to the second argument, USTR notes the Section 301 
   371  statute,
   372  
   373  [[Page 34275]]
   374  
   375  which governs these investigations, does not require the existence of 
   376  international standards discipling specific conduct as a prerequisite 
   377  to a finding of an unreasonable act, policy, or practice under Section 
   378  301(b) of the Trade Act. As explained in the Report, the definition of 
   379  unreasonable acts, policies, and practices in Section 301(d) 
   380  contemplates circumstances where, as here, acts, policies, and 
   381  practices of a foreign country may not be inconsistent with or violate 
   382  the international legal rights of the United States, but are 
   383  nevertheless unfair. Thus, the statutory structure of Section 301 
   384  contemplates that the Trade Representative may find unreasonable 
   385  conduct on the part of a trading partner even in the absence of 
   386  international standards or obligations.
   387      Third, some comments argued that where an economy has made 
   388  commitments to the United States regarding forced labor import 
   389  prohibitions, including through an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade, the 
   390  Trade Representative is without basis to find that same economy's 
   391  failure to impose and effectively enforce a forced labor import 
   392  prohibition is unreasonable. USTR applauds Argentina, Bangladesh, 
   393  Cambodia, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Indonesia, Malaysia, and 
   394  Taiwan, which have undertaken commitments regarding a forced labor 
   395  import prohibition. However, commitments to take action in the future 
   396  is distinct from forbidding legally the importation of forced labor 
   397  goods, and effectively enforcing such prohibition. Until such time as 
   398  the commitment is implemented, U.S. products will continue to compete 
   399  against forced labor products that have a competitive advantage in 
   400  global markets which, among other reasons explained in the Report, is 
   401  unreasonable.
   402      The Trade Representative fully expects economies that have 
   403  undertaken commitments related to prohibiting the importation of forced 
   404  labor goods to abide by those commitments. Accordingly, the Trade 
   405  Representative proposes that the additional duty rate to be applied in 
   406  the investigations take into account whether an economy has undertaken 
   407  such commitments.
   408  
   409  Response to Significant Comments Regarding Actions To Be Taken in the 
   410  Investigations
   411  
   412      A number of comments responded on potential responsive action by 
   413  the Trade Representative. These comments recommended that the Trade 
   414  Representative engage in multilateral negotiations, including at the 
   415  ILO, to encourage economies to impose a forced labor import prohibition 
   416  rather than take ``punitive measures,'' and to provide capacity 
   417  building and technical assistance, especially to developing economies, 
   418  to encourage effective enforcement of such a prohibition.
   419      The Trade Representative proposes that taking an action is 
   420  appropriate, and that action includes the imposition of additional 
   421  duties on products of the investigated economies, in order to obtain 
   422  the elimination of the investigated acts, policies, or practices. 
   423  However, the Trade Representative will continue to consider these 
   424  comments in conjunction with any action that might be taken with 
   425  respect to the investigations.
   426  
   427  VI. Request for Public Comments
   428  
   429      In accordance with section 304(b) of the Trade Act (19 U.S.C. 
   430  2414(b)), USTR invites comments from interested persons with respect to 
   431  the proposed actions to be taken in the investigations. To be assured 
   432  of consideration, you must submit written comments on the proposed 
   433  actions by July 6, 2026, in accordance with the instructions in section 
   434  VIII below.
   435      With respect to the proposed action, USTR invites comments 
   436  regarding:
   437       The specific products to be subject to increased duties, 
   438  including whether products should be retained or removed from the scope 
   439  of the action, or whether products currently listed in Annex A should 
   440  be added to the scope of the action;
   441       Whether products listed in Annex A are appropriately 
   442  excluded;
   443       The level of the increase, if any, in the rate of duty;
   444       Whether different tariff rates should be applied to an 
   445  economy where the economy has made a commitment to the United States to 
   446  impose and enforce a forced labor import prohibition; has imposed a 
   447  forced labor import prohibition; or has imposed a partial regime with 
   448  the effect of preventing the importation of certain forced labor goods.
   449       Features of a textile mechanism, including the U.S. and 
   450  foreign products to be covered, the relative market opportunities for 
   451  each side, and the tariff rate (if any) to be applied to products 
   452  subject to that mechanism, as well as whether a similar mechanism 
   453  should apply to any other product or sector.
   454      In considering whether certain articles should be subject to 
   455  additional duties under Section 301, USTR will consider the needs of 
   456  the U.S. economy. In commenting on the inclusion or removal of 
   457  particular tariff subheadings subject to the proposed action, USTR 
   458  requests that comments address specifically whether the products under 
   459  the tariff subheading are necessary raw materials that if subject to 
   460  the proposed additional tariffs could lead to the unavailability of 
   461  domestic supply; whether additional tariffs would cause serious 
   462  dislocations in the supply of the products and could cause economy-wide 
   463  disruptions, or other similar factors; and whether imposing additional 
   464  tariffs on products under the tariff subheading would be practicable or 
   465  effective in obtaining the elimination of the investigated acts, 
   466  policies, and practices.
   467      Additional instructions on how to submit written comments are 
   468  provided in section VIII below.
   469  
   470  VII. Hearing Participation
   471  
   472      The Section 301 Committee will convene public hearings beginning on 
   473  July 7, 2026, in the main hearing room of the U.S. International Trade 
   474  Commission, 500 E Street SW, Washington, DC 20436, beginning at 10:00 
   475  a.m. The hearings may continue, as appropriate. To testify at the 
   476  hearings, you must submit a request to appear using the electronic 
   477  portal at https://comments.ustr.gov/s/, following the instructions in 
   478  Part VIII below.
   479      Requests to appear must include a summary of testimony, and may be 
   480  accompanied by a pre-hearing submission. USTR will announce details of 
   481  the hearing at a later time. All submissions must be in English. To be 
   482  assured of consideration, USTR must receive your request to appear and 
   483  summary of the testimony by June 22, 2026.
   484  
   485  VIII. Procedures for Written Comments
   486  
   487      You must submit requests to appear at the hearings or written 
   488  comments using the appropriate docket on the portal at https://comments.ustr.gov/s/. All submissions must be in English.
   489      Interested persons wishing to provide testimony at the hearings 
   490  must submit a notification of intent and summary of testimony using the 
   491  docket entitled ``Request to Appear at the Hearing on Proposed Action 
   492  in the Section 301 Investigations of Acts, Policies, and Practices of 
   493  Various Economies Related to the Failure to Impose and Effectively 
   494  Enforce a Prohibition on the Importation of Goods Produced with Forced 
   495  Labor,'' docket number USTR-2026-0266.
   496      To submit written comments, including rebuttal comments, use the 
   497  docket on the portal entitled ``Request for Comments Concerning 
   498  Proposed Action in Section 301 Investigations of Various Economies 
   499  Related to the Failure to Impose and Effectively
   500  
   501  [[Page 34276]]
   502  
   503  Enforce a Prohibition on the Importation of Goods Produced with Forced 
   504  Labor Rights'', docket number USTR-2026-0265.
   505      You do not need to establish an account to submit comments. The 
   506  first screen of each docket allows you to enter identification and 
   507  contact information. Third party organizations such as law firms, trade 
   508  associations, or customs brokers, should identify the full legal name 
   509  of the organization they represent, and identify the primary point of 
   510  contact for the submission. Information fields are optional; however, 
   511  your comment or request may not be considered if insufficient 
   512  information is provided.
   513      Fields with a gray Business Confidential Information (BCI) notation 
   514  are for BCI information which will not be made publicly available. 
   515  Fields with a green (Public) notation will be viewable by the public.
   516      After entering the identification and contact information, you can 
   517  complete the remainder of the comment, or any portion of it by clicking 
   518  ``Next.'' You may upload documents at the end of the form and indicate 
   519  whether USTR should treat the documents as business confidential or 
   520  public information.
   521      Any page containing BCI must be clearly marked `BUSINESS 
   522  CONFIDENTIAL' on the top of that page and the submission should clearly 
   523  indicate, via brackets, highlighting, or other means, the specific 
   524  information that is BCI. If you request business confidential 
   525  treatment, you must certify in writing that disclosure of the 
   526  information would endanger trade secrets or profitability, and that the 
   527  information would not customarily be released to the public.
   528      Parties uploading attachments containing BCI also must submit a

    60                  Government of Iran), I declared or described national 
    61                  emergencies with respect to unusual and extraordinary 
    62                  threats to the national security, foreign policy, or 
    63                  economy of the United States and took actions to deal 
    64                  with those threats, including by imposing, pursuant to

    66                  of certain foreign trading partners.

    68                  In light of recent events, the additional ad valorem 
    69                  duties imposed pursuant to IEEPA in Executive Order 
    70                  14193, as amended; Executive Order 14194, as amended; 
    71                  Executive Order 14195, as amended; Executive Order 
    72                  14245; Executive Order 14257, as amended; Executive 
    73                  Order 14323, as amended; Executive Order 14329, as 
    74                  amended; Executive Order 14380; and Executive Order 
    75                  14382 shall no longer be in effect and, as soon as 
    76                  practicable, shall no longer be collected. All other 
    77                  actions, including any other action taken to address 
    78                  the national emergencies declared or described in 
    79                  Executive Order 14193, Executive Order 14194, Executive 
    80                  Order 14195, Executive Order 14245, Executive Order 
    81                  14257, Executive Order 14323, Executive Order 14329,

    42                  I, DONALD J. TRUMP, President of the United States of

    46                  strain on our healthcare system, public services, and

    49                  This challenge threatens the fabric of our society.

    51                  drugs of all kinds have poured across our borders and

    53                  in these challenges, including by failing to devote

    58                  Drug trafficking organizations (DTOs) are the world's

    64                  transnational cartels to smuggle illicit drugs into the 
    65                  United States, utilizing clandestine airstrips,

    68                  The challenges at our southern border are foremost in

    73                  our northern border. There is also a growing presence 
    74                  of Mexican cartels operating fentanyl and nitazene

    77                  distribution networks and international mail--due, in

    79                  exemption from duty and taxes, also known as de

    82                  States, as outlined in the Presidential Memorandum of

    86                  Organizations and Specially Designated Global

    28                  By the authority vested in me as President by the

    33                  section 604 of the Trade Act of 1974, as amended (19 
    34                  U.S.C. 2483), and section 301 of title 3, United States 
    35                  Code, it is hereby ordered:
    36  
    37                  Section 1. Background. On February 1, 2025, I 
    38                  determined that the failure of Canada to arrest, seize, 
    39                  detain, or otherwise intercept drug trafficking 
    40                  organizations, other drug and human traffickers, 
    41                  criminals at large, and illicit drugs constitutes an 
    42                  unusual and extraordinary threat, which has its source 
    43                  in substantial part outside the United States, to the 
    44                  national security, foreign policy, and economy of the 
    45                  United States. To address that threat, I invoked my 
    46                  authority under section 1702(a)(1)(B) of IEEPA to 
    47                  impose ad valorem tariffs on articles that are products 
    48                  of Canada.
    49  
    50                  Sec. 2. Immediate Steps. Pursuant to section 3 of my 
    51                  Executive Order of February 1, 2025, titled ``Imposing 
    52                  Duties to Address the Situation at Our Northern 
    53                  Border'' (``the Executive Order of February 1, 2025''), 
    54                  I have determined that the Government of Canada has 
    55                  taken immediate steps designed to alleviate the illegal 
    56                  migration and illicit drug crisis through cooperative 
    57                  actions. Further time is needed, however, to assess 
    58                  whether these steps constitute sufficient action to 
    59                  alleviate the crisis and resolve the unusual and 
    60                  extraordinary threat beyond our northern border.
    61  
    62                  Sec. 3. Pause. (a) In recognition of the steps taken by 
    63                  the Government of Canada, and in order to assess 
    64                  whether the threat described in section 1 of this order 
    65                  has abated, the additional 25 percent ad valorem rates 
    66                  of duty, and 10 percent ad valorem rates of duty as to 
    67                  energy products, shall be paused and will not take 
    68                  effect until March 4, 2025, at 12:01 a.m. eastern time. 
    69                  Accordingly, section 2(a), section 2(b), section 2(e), 
    70                  and section 2(f) of the Executive Order of February 1, 
    71                  2025, are amended by striking the term ``February 4, 
    72                  2025,'' where it appears in those sections and 
    73                  inserting in lieu thereof the term ``March 4, 2025.'' 
    74                  The exceptions set forth in section 2(a) and section 
    75                  2(b) of the Executive Order of February 1, 2025, 
    76                  related to covered goods loaded onto a vessel at a port 
    77                  of entry or in transit on the final mode of transport 
    78                  prior to entry into the United States are, hereby, 
    79                  withdrawn.
    80  
    81                      (b) During this pause, the Secretary of Homeland 
    82                  Security, in consultation with the Secretary of State, 
    83                  the Attorney General, the Assistant to the President 
    84                  for National Security Affairs, and the Assistant to the 
    85                  President for Homeland Security shall continue to 
    86                  assess the situation at our northern border, as
