    65                  Executive Order 14325 of July 31, 2025
    66  
    67                  
    68  Amendment to Duties To Address the Flow of 
    69                  Illicit Drugs Across Our Northern Border
    70  
    71                  By the authority vested in me as President by the 
    72                  Constitution and the laws of the United States of 
    73                  America, including the International Emergency Economic 
    74                  Powers Act (50 U.S.C. 1701 et seq.) (IEEPA), the 
    75                  National Emergencies Act (50 U.S.C. 1601 et seq.), 
    76                  section 604 of the Trade Act of 1974, as amended (19 
    77                  U.S.C. 2483), and section 301 of title 3, United States 
    78                  Code, I hereby determine and order:
    79  
    80                  Section 1. Background. In Executive Order 14193 of 
    81                  February 1, 2025 (Imposing Duties To Address the Flow 
    82                  of Illicit Drugs Across Our Northern Border), I 
    83                  declared a national emergency arising from certain 
    84                  conditions, including the public health crisis caused 
    85                  by fentanyl and other illicit drugs, and the failure of 
    86                  Canada to do more to arrest, seize, detain, or 
    87                  otherwise intercept drug trafficking organizations, 
    88                  other drug or human traffickers, criminals at large, 
    89                  and illicit drugs. In that order, I found that those 
    90                  conditions constitute an unusual and extraordinary 
    91                  threat, which has its source in substantial part 
    92                  outside the United States, to the national security, 
    93                  foreign policy, and economy of the United States.
    94  
    95                  To deal with the emergency declared in Executive Order 
    96                  14193, I imposed an additional ad valorem rate of duty 
    97                  of 25 percent on certain articles that are products of 
    98                  Canada and an additional ad valorem rate of duty of 10 
    99                  percent on certain energy or energy resources that are 
   100                  products of Canada. In Executive Order 14231 of March 
   101                  6, 2025 (Amendment to Duties To Address the Flow of 
   102                  Illicit Drugs Across Our Northern Border), I provided 
   103                  that the additional ad valorem rates of duties under 
   104                  Executive Order 14193 do not apply to articles that are 
   105                  products of Canada that qualify for duty-free entry 
   106                  under the Agreement between the United States of 
   107                  America, United Mexican States, and Canada (USMCA), and 
   108                  I reduced the additional ad valorem rate of duty on 
   109                  potash from 25 percent to 10 percent.
   110  
   111                  Section 2(d) of Executive Order 14193 provides that 
   112                  ``[s]hould Canada retaliate against the United States . 
   113                  . . through import duties on United States exports to 
   114                  Canada or similar measures,'' I ``may increase or 
   115                  expand in scope the duties imposed . . . to ensure the 
   116                  efficacy of th[e] action'' taken in Executive Order 
   117                  14193. Section 3(b) of Executive Order 14193 provides 
   118                  that the Secretary of Homeland Security, in 
   119                  coordination with other senior officials, ``shall 
   120                  recommend additional action, if necessary, should the 
   121                  Government of Canada fail to take adequate steps to 
   122                  alleviate the illegal migration and illicit drug crises 
   123                  through cooperative enforcement actions.''
   124  
   125                  I have received additional information and 
   126                  recommendations from various senior officials 
   127                  regarding, among other things, Canada's lack of 
   128                  cooperation in stemming the flood of fentanyl and other 
   129                  illicit drugs across our northern border--including its 
   130                  failure to devote satisfactory resources to arrest, 
   131                  seize, detain, or otherwise intercept drug trafficking 
   132                  organizations, other drug or human traffickers, 
   133                  criminals at large, and illicit drugs--and Canada's 
   134                  efforts to retaliate against the United States in 
   135                  response to Executive Order 14193, as amended. After 
   136                  considering the additional information and 
   137                  recommendations that I have received, among other 
   138                  things, I have determined that, for the products of 
   139                  Canada that are subject to the additional ad valorem 
   140                  rate of duty of 25 percent, the additional ad valorem 
   141                  rate of duty shall increase from 25 percent to 35 
   142                  percent. In my judgment, this action is
   143  
   144  [[Page 37958]]
   145  
   146                  necessary and appropriate to deal with the emergency 
   147                  declared in Executive Order 14193.
   148  
   149                  Sec. 2. Implementation. (a) All articles that are 
   150                  subject to the additional ad valorem rate of duty of 25 
   151                  percent under Executive Order 14193, as amended, shall 
   152                  instead be subject to an additional ad valorem rate of 
   153                  duty of 35 percent. Accordingly, the Harmonized Tariff 
   154                  Schedule of the United States (HTSUS) shall be modified 
   155                  as provided in the Annex to this order.
   156  
   157                      (b) The changes set forth herein shall be effective 
   158                  with respect to goods entered for consumption, or 
   159                  withdrawn from warehouse for consumption, on or after 
   160                  12:01 a.m. eastern daylight time on August 1, 2025.
   161                      (c) Nothing in this order shall be construed to 
   162                  alter or otherwise affect section 2(b) of Executive 
   163                  Order 14193 or section 2(a) or section 2(b) of 
   164                  Executive Order 14231.
   165                      (d) The stacking rules set out in Executive Order 
   166                  14289 of April 29, 2025 (Addressing Certain Tariffs on 
   167                  Imported Articles), and any subsequent order or 
   168                  proclamation addressing stacking of tariffs imposed 
   169                  under IEEPA, shall continue to apply to goods that are 
   170                  subject to subsection (a) of this section.
   171                      (e) The Secretary of Homeland Security, in 
   172                  consultation with the United States International Trade 
   173                  Commission, shall determine whether any additional 
   174                  modifications to the HTSUS are necessary to effectuate 
   175                  this order and may make such modifications through 
   176                  notice in the Federal Register.
   177  
   178                  Sec. 3. Transshipment. (a) All articles of Canada that 
   179                  do not qualify as originating under USMCA and are 
   180                  determined by U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) 
   181                  to have been transshipped to evade applicable duties 
   182                  under section 2 of this order shall be subject to (i) 
   183                  an additional ad valorem rate of duty of 40 percent, in 
   184                  lieu of the additional ad valorem rate of duty 
   185                  applicable under section 2 of this order to goods of 
   186                  the country of origin; (ii) any other applicable or 
   187                  appropriate fine or penalty, including those assessed 
   188                  under 19 U.S.C. 1592; and (iii) any other United States 
   189                  duties, fees, taxes, exactions, or charges applicable 
   190                  to goods of the country of origin. CBP shall not allow, 
   191                  consistent with applicable law, for mitigation or 
   192                  remission of the penalties assessed on imports found to 
   193                  be transshipped to evade applicable duties.
   194  
   195                      (b) The Secretary of Commerce and the Secretary of 
   196                  Homeland Security, acting through the Commissioner of 
   197                  CBP, in consultation with the United States Trade 
   198                  Representative, shall publish every 6 months a list of 
   199                  countries and specific facilities used in circumvention 
   200                  schemes, to inform public procurement, national 
   201                  security reviews, and commercial due diligence.
   202  
   203                  Sec. 4. Monitoring and Recommendations. (a) The 
   204                  Secretary of Homeland Security shall continue to 
   205                  monitor, and regularly consult with the Secretary of 
   206                  State, the Attorney General, the Assistant to the 
   207                  President for National Security Affairs, and the 
   208                  Assistant to the President for Homeland Security, on 
   209                  the situation at our northern border. The Secretary of 
   210                  Homeland Security shall inform the President of any 
   211                  circumstances that, in her opinion, might indicate the 
   212                  need for further action by the President. The Secretary 
   213                  of Homeland Security shall also inform the President of 
   214                  any circumstance that, in her opinion, might indicate 
   215                  that the Government of Canada has taken adequate steps 
   216                  to alleviate the emergency declared in Executive Order 
   217                  14193.
   218  
   219                      (b) The Secretary of Homeland Security, in 
   220                  coordination with the Secretary of State, the Attorney 
   221                  General, the Assistant to the President for National 
   222                  Security Affairs, and the Assistant to the President 
   223                  for Homeland Security, shall recommend additional 
   224                  action, if necessary, should the Government of Canada 
   225                  fail to take adequate steps to alleviate the illicit 
   226                  drug crisis or should the Government of Canada 
   227                  retaliate against the United States in response to the 
   228                  actions taken in Executive Order 14193 or any 
   229                  subsequent order issued to address the emergency 
   230                  declared in Executive Order 14193.
   231  
   232                  Sec. 5. Delegation. The Secretary of Homeland Security, 
   233                  in consultation with the Secretary of the Treasury, the 
   234                  Attorney General, and the Secretary
   235  
   236  [[Page 37959]]
   237  
   238                  of Commerce, is hereby authorized to take such actions, 
   239                  including adopting rules and regulations, and to employ 
   240                  all powers granted to the President by IEEPA as may be 
   241                  necessary to implement this order. The Secretary of 
   242                  Homeland Security may, consistent with applicable law, 
   243                  redelegate any of these functions within the Department 
   244                  of Homeland Security. All executive departments and 
   245                  agencies shall take all appropriate measures within 
   246                  their authority to implement this order.
   247  
   248                  Sec. 6. Severability. If any provision of this order, 
   249                  or the application of any provision of this order to 
   250                  any individual or circumstance, is held to be invalid, 
   251                  the remainder of this order and the application of its 
   252                  provisions to any other individuals or circumstances 
   253                  shall not be affected.
   254  
   255                  Sec. 7. General Provisions. (a) Nothing in this order 
   256                  shall be construed to impair or otherwise affect:
   257  
   258  (i) the authority granted by law to an executive department or agency, or 
   259  the head thereof; or
   260  
   261  (ii) the functions of the Director of the Office of Management and Budget 
   262  relating to budgetary, administrative, or legislative proposals.
   263  
   264                      (b) This order shall be implemented consistent with 
   265                  applicable law and subject to the availability of 
   266                  appropriations.
   267                      (c) This order is not intended to, and does not, 
   268                  create any right or benefit, substantive or procedural, 
   269                  enforceable at law or in equity by any party against 
   270                  the United States, its departments, agencies, or 
   271                  entities, its officers, employees, or agents, or any 
   272                  other person.
   273                      (d) The costs for publication of this order shall 
   274                  be borne by the Department of Homeland Security.

    23                  Executive Order 14289 of April 29, 2025
    24

    26  Addressing Certain Tariffs on Imported Articles
    27  
    28                  By the authority vested in me as President by the 
    29                  Constitution and the laws of the United States of 
    30                  America, including the International Emergency Economic 
    31                  Powers Act (50 U.S.C. 1701 et seq.), the National 
    32                  Emergencies Act (50 U.S.C. 1601 et seq.), section 604 
    33                  of the Trade Act of 1974, as amended (19 U.S.C. 2483), 
    34                  section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962, as 
    35                  amended (19 U.S.C. 1862), and section 301 of title 3, 
    36                  United States Code, it is hereby ordered:
    37  
    38                  Section 1. Purpose. The United States has imposed 
    39                  tariffs under various statutory authorities and through 
    40                  a number of Executive Orders and proclamations to 
    41                  protect national security and address unusual and 
    42                  extraordinary threats to the national security, foreign 
    43                  policy, and economy of the United States. Although each 
    44                  of these actions, as listed in section 2 of this order, 
    45                  serves separate and distinct policy purposes, I have 
    46                  now determined that, to the extent these tariffs apply 
    47                  to the same article, these tariffs should not all have 
    48                  a cumulative effect (or ``stack'' on top of one 
    49                  another) because the rate of duty resulting from such 
    50                  stacking exceeds what is necessary to achieve the 
    51                  intended policy goals. To avoid the cumulative effect 
    52                  of overlapping tariffs on certain articles, this order 
    53                  sets out the procedure for determining which of 
    54                  multiple tariffs shall apply to an article when that 
    55                  article is subject to more than one of the actions 
    56                  listed in section 2 of this order.
    57  
    58                  Sec. 2. Applicability. This order shall apply only to 
    59                  the administration of tariffs imposed through the 
    60                  following actions and subsequent amendments to those 
    61                  tariffs:
    62  
    63                      (a) Proclamation 10908 of March 26, 2025 (Adjusting 
    64                  Imports of Automobiles and Automobile Parts Into the 
    65                  United States);
    66                      (b) Executive Order 14193 of February 1, 2025 
    67                  (Imposing Duties To Address the Flow of Illicit Drugs 
    68                  Across Our Northern Border), as amended by Executive 
    69                  Order 14197 of February 3, 2025 (Progress on the 
    70                  Situation at Our Northern Border), Executive Order 
    71                  14226 of March 2, 2025 (Amendment to Duties To Address 
    72                  the Flow of Illicit Drugs Across Our Northern Border), 
    73                  and Executive Order 14231 of March 6, 2025 (Amendment 
    74                  to Duties to Address the Flow of Illicit Drugs Across 
    75                  Our Northern Border);
    76                      (c) Executive Order 14194 of February 1, 2025 
    77                  (Imposing Duties To Address the Situation at Our 
    78                  Southern Border), as amended by Executive Order 14198 
    79                  of February 3, 2025 (Progress on the Situation at Our 
    80                  Southern Border), Executive Order 14227 of March 2, 
    81                  2025 (Amendment to Duties To Address the Situation at 
    82                  Our Southern Border), and Executive Order 14232 of 
    83                  March 6, 2025 (Amendment to Duties to Address the Flow 
    84                  of Illicit Drugs Across Our Southern Border);
    85                      (d) Proclamation 9704 of March 8, 2018 (Adjusting 
    86                  Imports of Aluminum Into the United States), as amended 
    87                  by Proclamation 9980 of January 24, 2020 (Adjusting 
    88                  Imports of Derivative Aluminum Articles and Derivative 
    89                  Steel Articles Into the United States), and 
    90                  Proclamation 10895 of February 10, 2025 (Adjusting 
    91                  Imports of Aluminum Into the United States); and
    92                      (e) Proclamation 9705 of March 8, 2018 (Adjusting 
    93                  Imports of Steel Into the United States), as amended by 
    94                  Proclamation 9980 of January 24, 2020 (Adjusting 
    95                  Imports of Derivative Aluminum Articles and Derivative 
    96                  Steel
    97  
    98  [[Page 18908]]
    99  
   100                  Articles Into the United States), and Proclamation 
   101                  10896 of February 10, 2025 (Adjusting Imports of Steel 
   102                  Into the United States).
   103  
   104                  Sec. 3. Non-Stacking of Tariff Measures. (a) 
   105                  Notwithstanding any provision of any action listed in 
   106                  section 2 of this order, tariffs for articles subject 
   107                  to tariffs under the actions listed in section 2 of 
   108                  this order shall apply as follows:
   109  
   110  (i) An article subject to tariffs pursuant to the action listed in section 
   111  (2)(a) of this order shall not be subject to additional tariffs on that 
   112  article pursuant to the actions listed in sections 2(b) through 2(e) of 
   113  this order.
   114  
   115  (ii) An article subject to tariffs pursuant to the actions listed in 
   116  section 2(b) or 2(c) of this order shall not be subject to additional 
   117  tariffs on that article pursuant to the actions listed in section 2(d) or 
   118  2(e) of this order.
   119  
   120  (iii) An article subject to tariffs pursuant to the actions listed in 
   121  section 2(d) of this order shall be subject to additional tariffs on that 
   122  article pursuant to the actions listed in section 2(e) of this order, 
   123  provided the article otherwise satisfies all conditions necessary for 
   124  application of those additional tariffs; likewise, an article subject to 
   125  tariffs pursuant to the actions listed in section 2(e) of this order shall 
   126  be subject to additional tariffs on that article pursuant to the actions 
   127  listed in section 2(d) of this order, provided the article otherwise 
   128  satisfies all conditions necessary for application of those additional 
   129  tariffs.
   130  
   131                      (b) Subsection (a) of this section shall not be 
   132                  construed to diminish the validity of any action listed 
   133                  in section 2 of this order. Each action listed in 
   134                  section 2 of this order remains independently valid and 
   135                  enforceable, except that the duty rates provided by 
   136                  these actions shall not be cumulative when the 
   137                  conditions outlined in subsection (a) of this section 
   138                  are met.
   139                      (c) If an imported article is subject to both a 
   140                  tariff imposed pursuant to subsection (a) of this 
   141                  section and one or more tariffs imposed pursuant to an 
   142                  action or actions not listed in section 2 of this 
   143                  order, then the tariff imposed on the article pursuant 
   144                  to subsection (a) of this section shall be cumulative 
   145                  with the tariff or tariffs imposed pursuant to the 
   146                  action or actions not listed in section 2 of this 
   147                  order.
   148  
   149                  Sec. 4. Non-applicability to Other Tariff Measures. (a) 
   150                  Nothing in this order shall be interpreted to alter or 
   151                  limit the application of any duties, taxes, fees, or 
   152                  exactions other than those imposed pursuant to the 
   153                  actions listed in section 2 of this order.
   154  
   155                      (b) Accordingly, an article that is subject to 
   156                  duties pursuant to an action listed in section 2 of 
   157                  this order may still be subject to other applicable 
   158                  duties, taxes, fees, exactions, and charges, such as, 
   159                  but not limited to, those set forth in column 1 of the 
   160                  Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States 
   161                  (HTSUS); duties imposed pursuant to section 301 of the 
   162                  Trade Act of 1974, as amended; duties imposed pursuant 
   163                  to Executive Order 14195 of February 1, 2025 (Imposing 
   164                  Duties To Address the Synthetic Opioid Supply Chain in 
   165                  the People's Republic of China), as amended; and 
   166                  antidumping and countervailing duties.
   167  
   168                  Sec. 5. Implementation. (a) The Secretary of Homeland 
   169                  Security, acting through the Commissioner of U.S. 
   170                  Customs and Border Protection and in consultation with

tools.name: fr_search

query.description: Full-text search terms; "" for none. Supports quoted phrases, e.g. "\"extension of stay\" F-1".
query.title: Query

doc_type.description: Document types: RULE, PRORULE (proposed rule), NOTICE, PRESDOCU (presidential document). null for all.

agency.description: Agency slugs, e.g. homeland-security-department, u-s-citizenship-and-immigration-services, u-s-immigration-and-customs-enforcement, state-department, labor-department, executive-office-of-the-president.

pres_type.description: Presidential document subtypes (use with doc_type PRESDOCU).

cfr.description: CFR title:part affected, e.g. 8:214. The part must be numeric; lettered parts are not supported by this filter.
cfr.title: Cfr

tools.description: Search U.S. Federal Register documents (rules, proposed rules, notices, presidential documents) by keywords and filters. Prints document numbers, titles, types, dates, citations, dockets, RINs and abstracts.

tools.name: fr_doc
tools.description: Metadata for one Federal Register document: title, type, action, citation, page range, publication/signing/effective dates, comment deadline, docket, RIN, CFR parts affected, corrections, abstract.

tools.name: fr_toc
tools.description: Outline of a document's full text: headings with line numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_grep

pattern.description: Python regular expression, searched over the whole text (a match may span lines). ^ and $ match at line boundaries; . does not match a newline.

context.description: Lines of context around each match (default 2, at most 10).
context.title: Context

tools.description: Regex search inside one document's full text. Shows the lines of each match with line numbers, context lines and the FR page of each match. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_text
tools.description: Read a document's full text by line range, with line numbers. [[Page N]] markers give FR page numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

answer.description: Direct answer to each lettered part, in order, labelled (a), (b), ...

basis.description: Provisions and documents relied on, with citations.

uncertainty.description: What the documents leave open, or "None".
uncertainty.title: Uncertainty

    90  Further Strengthening Actions Taken To Adjust 
    91                  Imports of Aluminum Into the United States
    92  
    93                  By the President of the United States of America
    94  
    95                  A Proclamation
    96  
    97                  1. In Proclamation 9704 of March 8, 2018 (Adjusting 
    98                  Imports of Aluminum Into the United States), as 
    99                  amended, I found, under section 232 of the Trade 
   100                  Expansion Act of 1962, as amended, 19 U.S.C. 1862 
   101                  (section 232), that aluminum is being imported into the 
   102                  United States in such quantities or under such 
   103                  circumstances as to threaten to impair the national 
   104                  security of the United States. To address the national 
   105                  security threat found in Proclamation 9704, I 
   106                  established a tariff regime, which included imposing ad 
   107                  valorem duties on certain imports of aluminum articles 
   108                  and its derivative articles. In subsequent 
   109                  proclamations, including Proclamation 11021 of April 2, 
   110                  2026 (Strengthening Actions Taken To Adjust Imports of 
   111                  Aluminum, Steel, and Copper Into the United States), 
   112                  and Proclamation 11032 of June 1, 2026 (Further 
   113                  Adjusting the Tariff Regimes for Imports of Aluminum, 
   114                  Steel, and Copper Into the United States), I modified 
   115                  the tariff regime for aluminum to more effectively 
   116                  address the national security threat found in 
   117                  Proclamation 9704.
   118  
   119                  2. In those proclamations, I directed the Secretary of 
   120                  Commerce (Secretary) to monitor the effects of imports 
   121                  of aluminum with respect to the national security, to 
   122                  update me on the status of that threat to the national 
   123                  security, and to provide me with recommendations if 
   124                  circumstances indicated the need for further 
   125                  Presidential action under section 232.
   126  
   127                  3. Based on the Secretary's monitoring, I have received 
   128                  information, opinions, and recommendations from the 
   129                  Secretary regarding the tariff regime imposed in 
   130                  Proclamation 9704, as amended, and the national 
   131                  security threat found in Proclamation 9704.
   132  
   133                  4. Among other things, the Secretary has informed me 
   134                  that the additional ad valorem duties on imports of 
   135                  aluminum are strengthening the American aluminum 
   136                  industries and addressing the national security threat 
   137                  found in Proclamation 9704. In the Secretary's opinion, 
   138                  domestic aluminum production and related domestic 
   139                  aluminum industry would not be as strong as they are if 
   140                  not for the aluminum tariff regime imposed under 
   141                  section 232, and the national security threat found in 
   142                  Proclamation 9704 would be worse than it is if not for 
   143                  the aluminum tariff regime imposed under section 232.
   144  
   145                  5. The Secretary has informed and advised me of his 
   146                  opinion that, despite the benefits from the aluminum 
   147                  tariff regime, the domestic production and supply of 
   148                  primary aluminum, which is critical to the U.S. economy 
   149                  and defense industrial base, is still in insufficient 
   150                  supply. In the Secretary's view, it is important to 
   151                  modify the aluminum tariff regime in a way to more 
   152                  effectively encourage increased domestic production of 
   153                  primary aluminum.
   154  
   155                  6. To ensure that the aluminum tariff regime continues 
   156                  to effectively address the national security threat 
   157                  found in Proclamation 9704, the Secretary recommended 
   158                  that I establish an incentive for companies to engage 
   159                  in building new facilities capable of producing primary 
   160                  aluminum, expanding facilities
   161  
   162  [[Page 46636]]
   163  
   164                  to become capable of producing primary aluminum, or 
   165                  refurbishing outdated facilities that produce primary 
   166                  aluminum to expand their production or increase the 
   167                  efficiency of production. The Secretary recommended 
   168                  that I do this by allowing those companies or their 
   169                  designated representatives to import a quantity of 
   170                  primary aluminum corresponding to the reasonably 
   171                  anticipated annual production of primary aluminum from 
   172                  the new project at a reduced tariff rate. This would 
   173                  build on the program established for certain aluminum 
   174                  and steel from Canada and Mexico in clause 13 of 
   175                  Proclamation 10984 of October 17, 2025 (Adjusting 
   176                  Imports of Medium- and Heavy-Duty Vehicles, Medium- and 
   177                  Heavy-Duty Vehicle Parts, and Buses Into the United 
   178                  States).
   179  
   180                  7. After considering the current information, opinions, 
   181                  and recommendations newly provided by the Secretary; 
   182                  the factors in section 232 (19 U.S.C. 1862(d)); the 
   183                  need to address the national security threat found in 
   184                  Proclamation 9704; and other relevant factors and 
   185                  information, I have determined that it is necessary and 
   186                  appropriate to modify the tariff regime for imports of 
   187                  aluminum imposed in Proclamation 9704, as amended. In 
   188                  particular, I determine that it is necessary and 
   189                  appropriate to establish an investment incentive 
   190                  program for companies investing in new U.S. production 
   191                  capacity for primary aluminum, as further detailed 
   192                  below. In my judgment, the modifications in this 
   193                  proclamation will ensure that the tariff regime imposed 
   194                  on imports of aluminum continue to effectively address 
   195                  the national security threat found in Proclamation 
   196                  9704.
   197  
   198                  8. Section 232 authorizes the President to adjust the 
   199                  imports of an article and its derivatives that are 
   200                  being imported into the United States in such 
   201                  quantities or under such circumstances as to threaten 
   202                  to impair the national security of the United States so 
   203                  that such imports will not threaten to impair the 
   204                  national security.
   205  
   206                  9. Section 604 of the Trade Act of 1974, as amended (19 
   207                  U.S.C. 2483) (section 604), authorizes the President to 
   208                  embody in the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United 
   209                  States (HTSUS) the substance of statutes affecting 
   210                  import treatment, and actions thereunder, including the 
   211                  removal, modification, continuance, or imposition of 
   212                  any rate of duty or other import restriction.
   213  
   214                  NOW, THEREFORE, I, DONALD J. TRUMP, President of the 
   215                  United States of America, by the authority vested in me 
   216                  by the Constitution and the laws of the United States, 
   217                  including section 232, section 604, and section 301 of 
   218                  title 3, United States Code, do hereby proclaim as 
   219                  follows:
   220  
   221  (1) The Secretary is authorized to and shall establish a program to 
   222  incentivize new investment in U.S. production facilities to produce primary 
   223  aluminum.
   224  
   225    (a) The Secretary is authorized to solicit and accept onshoring plans 
   226  from companies. Any onshoring plan shall at least include: a commitment, if 
   227  the plan is approved, to build, refurbish, or expand a facility in the 
   228  United States that will produce primary aluminum; a commitment that 
   229  construction will start by January 20, 2029; and any other relevant 
   230  information and analysis, including requirements set by the Secretary.
   231  
   232    (b) The Secretary is authorized to approve onshoring plans described in 
   233  subclause (a) of this clause. In determining whether an onshoring plan 
   234  qualifies for approval, the Secretary, in consultation with any senior 
   235  executive branch officials the Secretary deems appropriate, shall consider 
   236  all relevant factors he deems appropriate, such as the anticipated start 
   237  date of construction, whether the proposed plan's project timeline is 
   238  commercially reasonable, whether the proposed plan's project milestones are 
   239  commercially reasonable, the anticipated annual production of primary 
   240  aluminum from the onshoring project, whether the proposed plan's 
   241  anticipated costs and primary-aluminum production projections are 
   242  reasonable, and how the benefits of the reduced tariff rate will be 
   243  allocated between the applicants of the onshoring plan. When approving 
   244  onshoring plans, the Secretary shall act in a manner consistent with the 
   245  need to address the national security threat found in Proclamation 9704.
   246  
   247  [[Page 46637]]
   248  
   249    (c) If the Secretary approves a company's onshoring plan, the Secretary 
   250  shall allow the company to annually import primary aluminum of a quantity 
   251  that corresponds to the U.S. production facility's reasonably anticipated 
   252  annual output of primary aluminum when the onshoring project is completed, 
   253  at half the section 232 rate of duty otherwise in effect. Tariff 
   254  adjustments awarded for facility refurbishment shall only be granted to the 
   255  extent those adjustments correspond with the value of the company's 
   256  investment.
   257  
   258    (d) The Secretary is authorized to take all actions that he deems 
   259  appropriate to implement and effectuate this program, including, consistent 
   260  with applicable law, the issuance of regulations, rules, guidance, and 
   261  procedures. All approved onshoring plans shall be subject to monitoring and 
   262  enforcement by the Secretary. The Secretary may require that companies with 
   263  approved onshoring plans submit reports to the Department of Commerce to 
   264  ensure compliance with domestic manufacturing commitments, and he may 
   265  require that such reports be audited, including by external auditing firms. 
   266  Should the Secretary determine that a company is substantially failing to 
   267  meet its agreed-upon commitments that are the basis for granting the tariff 
   268  benefits detailed in this proclamation, the Secretary is authorized to 
   269  cease and rescind the tariff benefits awarded pursuant to this 
   270  proclamation. In cases where the executive branch assesses that a company 
   271  engaged in fraud or deliberately misled the United States Government with 
   272  respect to onshoring commitments, the rescission of tariff benefits can be 
   273  retroactive to the extent permitted by law, and the Secretary or the 
   274  Commissioner of U.S. Customs and Border Protection may collect the 
   275  additional tariffs owed because of the retroactive rescission of the tariff 
   276  benefits and impose any appropriate fines or penalties to the extent 
   277  consistent with applicable law.
   278  
   279  (2) The Secretary, in consultation with the Secretary of Homeland Security, 
   280  the United States Trade Representative, the Chairman of the United States 
   281  International Trade Commission, and any other senior official the Secretary 
   282  deems appropriate, shall determine whether any modifications to the HTSUS 
   283  are necessary to effectuate or implement this proclamation or any actions 
   284  taken pursuant to this proclamation, and shall make such modifications 
   285  through notice in the Federal Register.
   286  
   287  (3) The Secretary shall continue to monitor imports of aluminum and its 
   288  derivatives. The Secretary shall, from time to time, review the status of 
   289  aluminum and its derivative imports with respect to the national security. 
   290  The Secretary shall inform me of any circumstances that, in his opinion, 
   291  might indicate the need for further Presidential action under section 232. 
   292  The Secretary shall also inform me of any circumstance that, in his 
   293  opinion, might indicate that any of the actions taken under section 232 are 
   294  no longer necessary.
   295  
   296  (4) To the extent consistent with applicable law, the Secretary and the 
   297  Secretary of Homeland Security are directed and authorized to take all 
   298  actions that are appropriate to implement and effectuate this proclamation 
   299  and any actions contemplated by this proclamation--including through 
   300  amendment of regulations or through notices in the Federal Register and by 
   301  adopting rules, regulations, or guidance--and to employ all powers granted 
   302  to the President, including by section 232, as may be appropriate to 
   303  implement and effectuate this proclamation, including to make any technical 
   304  or ministerial corrections to any annexes to this proclamation. The head of 
   305  each executive department and agency (agency) may, consistent with 
   306  applicable law, including section 301 of title 3, United States Code, 
   307  redelegate the authority to take such appropriate measures within the 
   308  agency.
   309  
   310  (5) Any provision of previous proclamations and Executive Orders that is 
   311  inconsistent with this proclamation is superseded to the extent of such 
   312  inconsistency.
   313  
   314  [[Page 46638]]
   315  
   316  (6) If any provision of this proclamation or the application of any 
   317  provision of this proclamation to any individual or circumstance is held to 
   318  be invalid, the remainder of this proclamation and the application of its 
   319  provisions to any other individual or circumstance shall not be affected.
   320  
   321                  IN WITNESS WHEREOF, I have hereunto set my hand this 
   322                  twentieth day of July, in the year of our Lord two 
   323                  thousand twenty-six, and of the Independence of the 
   324                  United States of America the two hundred and fifty-
   325                  first.

  1322  III. USTR Responses to Significant Comments
  1323  
  1324      In response to the June 5, 2026 FRN, USTR received over 1,600 
  1325  written comments and heard testimony from over 100 witnesses. USTR and 
  1326  the Section 301 Committee reviewed, examined, and considered each 
  1327  comment and the public testimony. USTR responds below to significant 
  1328  issues raised in the public comments and hearings in response to the 
  1329  June 5, 2026 FRN and further explains the Trade Representative's 
  1330  determinations to take appropriate and feasible action under Section 
  1331  301(b) at the specific direction of the President. See 19 U.S.C. 
  1332  2411(b)(2).
  1333  
  1334  A. Response to Comments Regarding Prior Determinations on Actionability
  1335  
  1336      Multiple comments raised arguments taking issue with some or all of 
  1337  the conclusions the Trade Representative reached in his actionability 
  1338  finding and Report in these investigations. These include arguments 
  1339  that the Trade Representative failed to substantiate the existence of 
  1340  unreasonable acts, policies, or practices in each investigation, or 
  1341  that the Trade Representative failed to demonstrate a burden or 
  1342  restriction imposed by the acts, policies, and practices of each 
  1343  economy. With respect to these arguments and other arguments regarding 
  1344  the Trade Representative's earlier findings on actionability, the Trade 
  1345  Representative observes that any such arguments that were appropriately 
  1346  raised during the actionability phase of these investigations were 
  1347  addressed in the June 5, 2026 FRN or the related comprehensive Report. 
  1348  Moreover, the Trade Representative has taken into account all available 
  1349  information regarding the efforts of the investigated economies to 
  1350  impose and effectively enforce forced labor import prohibitions since 
  1351  the issuance of the June 5, 2026 FRN.
  1352  
  1353  B. Comments Regarding the Use of Tariffs and Tariff Rates
  1354  
  1355  1. Responses to Significant Comments Regarding the Appropriateness of 
  1356  the Additional Tariffs To Address the Acts, Policies, and Practices 
  1357  Under Investigation
  1358      A number of comments argued that the additional tariffs proposed in 
  1359  these investigations are not appropriate to achieve the elimination of 
  1360  the unreasonable acts, policies, or practices of each of the 
  1361  investigated economies. These comments argued, among other things, that 
  1362  additional tariffs would be unlikely to significantly lessen the use of 
  1363  forced labor. Other comments argued
  1364  
  1365  [[Page 47329]]
  1366  
  1367  that USTR should undertake diplomatic engagement or engage in technical 
  1368  assistance and capacity building in order to achieve the elimination of 
  1369  the acts, policies, or practices in these investigations.
  1370      With respect to the first argument, consistent with the specific 
  1371  direction of the President, the Trade Representative has determined to 
  1372  impose tariffs as a means to encourage the investigated economies to 
  1373  impose and effectively enforce a forced labor import ban. Further, USTR 
  1374  observes that since the initiation of the investigations and the 
  1375  announcement of the proposed tariff actions, various economies have 
  1376  imposed or are taking steps toward imposing a forced labor import 
  1377  prohibition. This serves to confirm that tariff action can help obtain 
  1378  the elimination of the investigated acts, policies, and practices. 
  1379  While the elimination of forced labor generally is not the aim of these 
  1380  Section 301 investigations, as observed in the Report, the prevalence 
  1381  of forced labor has increased in recent years. Existing efforts to 
  1382  address forced labor have proven inadequate to prevent this increase. 
  1383  As discussed in the Report in these investigations, it is well 
  1384  established that an effectively enforced forced labor import 
  1385  prohibition can lead to the remediation of significant instances of 
  1386  forced labor.
  1387      With respect to technical assistance and capacity building, we 
  1388  observe that such efforts on their own are unlikely to achieve the 
  1389  elimination of the unreasonable acts, policies, and practices. However, 
  1390  where an economy agrees to address the issue of forced labor imports, 
  1391  and seeks assistance to impose or effectively enforce such a 
  1392  prohibition, such activities will be more effective. As discussed 
  1393  above, trade-based measures, particularly tariffs, are encouraging 
  1394  economies to impose or take steps toward imposing a forced labor import 
  1395  prohibition.
  1396      While the Trade Representative has considered the arguments raised 
  1397  in the comments, the Trade Representative disagrees with the comments 
  1398  for the reasons discussed above. Furthermore, because the comments 
  1399  suggested alternative actions that are inconsistent with the specific 
  1400  direction of the President, the Trade Representative cannot accommodate 
  1401  them.
  1402  2. Response to Comments Regarding the Proposed Tariff Rates
  1403      USTR received several types of comments regarding the proposed 
  1404  rates of duty for each investigation. For example, multiple comments 
  1405  questioned whether a 10 or 12.5 percent duty would be significant 
  1406  enough to encourage economies to eliminate the investigated acts, 
  1407  policies, and practices. Some comments argued that the 2.5 percentage 
  1408  point difference between the two rates is not significant enough to 
  1409  encourage economies to eliminate the investigated acts, policies, or 
  1410  practices. Multiple comments argued for certain investigated economies 
  1411  to be excluded from the application of additional duties or be assigned 
  1412  a lower additional rate of duty, including where the economy has 
  1413  domestic laws prohibiting forced labor. Related to these arguments, 
  1414  certain other comments argued that it was not appropriate for economies 
  1415  that have made commitments regarding forced labor in ARTs to receive 
  1416  the same tariff rate as economies with a forced labor import 
  1417  prohibition, or economies that have taken steps towards enforcement of 
  1418  a forced labor import prohibition, or economies with partial regimes 
  1419  with the effect of preventing the importation of certain forced labor 
  1420  goods. USTR addresses each of these comments in turn.
  1421      With respect to the significance of the rates of duty in these 
  1422  investigations, including the differential of 2.5 percentage points, 
  1423  the Trade Representative has determined that the rate for each economy 
  1424  is appropriate to obtain the elimination of that economy's acts, 
  1425  policies, and practices at this time. The Trade Representative 
  1426  considers that a lower rate of duty would not be appropriate to obtain 
  1427  the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices, at this time. The 
  1428  specific action and level of duty that will obtain the elimination of 
  1429  an act, policy, or practice is a matter of judgment, to be exercised by 
  1430  the Trade Representative, subject to any specific direction of the 
  1431  President. Information available indicates that these tariff rates and 
  1432  the differential between them are significant enough to spur action by 
  1433  investigated economies. Since the publication of the proposed actions 
  1434  in these investigations, a number of economies have either imposed 
  1435  forced labor import prohibitions, or undertaken a commitment to impose 
  1436  a forced labor import prohibition as part of an ART. Other economies 
  1437  have informed USTR that they are in the process of developing such 
  1438  measures. Accordingly, the rates and the differential between them have 
  1439  been successful in encouraging investigated economies to take steps 
  1440  toward eliminating the investigated acts, policies, and practices.
  1441      With respect to excluding economies or providing a lower rate of 
  1442  duty based on those economies' efforts to address forced labor within 
  1443  their jurisdictions, such as the ratification of International Labor 
  1444  Organization (ILO) conventions or domestic enforcement efforts related 
  1445  to forced labor, doing so would not achieve the elimination of the 
  1446  investigated acts, policies, and practices. The Trade Representative 
  1447  applauds the efforts of our trading partners to eliminate forced labor 
  1448  within their jurisdictions; however, as discussed in our June 5, 2026 
  1449  FRN and the related Report, these efforts are not pertinent to the 
  1450  elimination of the acts, policies, and practices that are the subject 
  1451  of these investigations.
  1452      With respect to excluding or providing a lower rate to economies 
  1453  that are in the process of developing forced labor import prohibitions, 
  1454  the mere development or proposal of a measure to prohibit the 
  1455  importation of forced labor goods, absent adoption of such measure, is 
  1456  insufficient to address the acts, policies, and practices that are the 
  1457  subject of these investigations. The development or proposal of such 
  1458  measures alone provides no guarantee that a forced labor import 
  1459  prohibition will be adopted and effectively enforced. Further, this is 
  1460  distinct from circumstances where an economy has taken on a concrete 
  1461  obligation to prohibit the importation of goods. Certain comments 
  1462  contend that the Trade Representative should assign different rates of 
  1463  duty to each of the following groups of economies: (1) those that have 
  1464  imposed forced labor import prohibitions; (2) those that made 
  1465  commitments regarding forced labor in an ART or other similar 
  1466  agreement; and (3) those that have imposed a partial regime with the 
  1467  effect of preventing the importation of certain forced labor goods. In 
  1468  the Trade Representative's judgment, imposing distinct tariff rates on 
  1469  each of these groups at this time would hinder the ability of the Trade 
  1470  Representative to achieve the elimination of the investigated acts, 
  1471  policies, and practices. The Trade Representative's determination to 
  1472  apply a lower rate of duty to each economy meeting these criteria 
  1473  acknowledges significant steps such economies are taking toward 
  1474  imposing and effectively enforcing forced labor import prohibitions.
  1475      Considering the public comments and the advice of the Section 301 
  1476  Committee, as well as the advice of advisory committees, and consistent 
  1477  with the specific direction of the President, the Trade Representative 
  1478  has determined that it is appropriate to impose tariffs of 10 percent 
  1479  or 10 percent net of MFN duties, based on whether an economy has 
  1480  imposed a
  1481  
  1482  [[Page 47330]]
  1483  
  1484  forced labor import prohibition, has undertaken commitments in an ART 
  1485  regarding forced labor import prohibition, or has imposed a partial 
  1486  regime with the effect of preventing the importation of certain forced 
  1487  labor goods, and has determined that it is appropriate to impose 
  1488  tariffs of 12.5 percent or 12.5 percent net of MFN duties for each 
  1489  other investigated economy. In the Trade Representative's judgment, 
  1490  imposing an economy-wide rate of zero or lower than 10 percent on 
  1491  economies that have entered into an ART without implementing a forced 
  1492  labor import prohibition, or on economies that have imposed a 
  1493  prohibition but do not yet effectively implement such prohibition, 
  1494  would be ineffective in encouraging the elimination of the acts, 
  1495  policies, and practices under investigation. While the Trade 
  1496  Representative has considered the arguments raised in the comments, the 
  1497  Trade Representative disagrees with the comments for the reasons 
  1498  discussed above. Furthermore, because the comments suggested 
  1499  alternative actions that are inconsistent with the specific direction 
  1500  of the President, the Trade Representative cannot accommodate them.
  1501  3. Response to Comments Urging Lower Tariff Rates in Investigations of 
  1502  Economies With Perceived Low-Risk Supply
  1503      Multiple comments suggested that the Trade Representative should 
  1504  impose a lower or zero tariff rate on economies with export industries 
  1505  that have a low-risk of forced labor in their supply chains. For 
  1506  example, certain commenters argued that where investigated economies 
  1507  export products to major U.S. retailers with their own supply chain due 
  1508  diligence procedures, additional tariffs on such products would be 
  1509  ineffective in bringing about the elimination of the investigated acts, 
  1510  policies, and practices. These comments misunderstand the aims of the 
  1511  investigations and the use of tariffs as leverage.
  1512      As demonstrated throughout the investigations, including in the 
  1513  Report, the investigations are broader than any particular industry or 
  1514  supply chain. The aim of each investigation is to encourage that 
  1515  economy to impose and effectively enforce a forced labor import 
  1516  prohibition. As already seen in certain investigations to date, tariffs 
  1517  have proved to be an effective point of leverage to encourage the 
  1518  elimination of the investigated acts, policies, and practices. Even 
  1519  accepting these arguments at face value, it does not follow that U.S. 
  1520  products do not compete in those economies against other imports 
  1521  manufactured with forced labor, or that other exports from those 
  1522  economies (i.e., those not subject to supply chain due diligence 
  1523  procedures) are not manufactured with imported inputs made with forced 
  1524  labor. While the Trade Representative has considered the arguments 
  1525  raised in the comments, the Trade Representative disagrees with the 
  1526  comments for the reasons discussed above. Furthermore, because the 
  1527  comments suggested alternative actions that are inconsistent with the 
  1528  specific direction of the President, the Trade Representative cannot 
  1529  accommodate them.
  1530  
  1531  C. Discussion of Comments on Proposed Product Exemptions
  1532  
  1533      USTR received a variety of comments on the proposed exemption list, 
  1534  including support for the products proposed for exemption and requests 
  1535  to remove certain products from the proposed exemption list. 
  1536  Considering the public comments and the advice of the Section 301 
  1537  Committee, as well as the advice of advisory committees and in 
  1538  accordance with the specific direction of the President, the Trade 
  1539  Representative has determined to exempt all of the products proposed 
  1540  for exemption in Annex A to the June 5, 2026 FRN, except the non-
  1541  pharmaceutical applications of certain chemical products. Other than 
  1542  the products with non-pharmaceutical applications, as discussed below, 
  1543  the Trade Representative determined not to remove additional products 
  1544  from the exemption list. The Trade Representative determined to exempt 
  1545  certain additional products not included in the proposed exemptions in 
  1546  Annex A to June 5, 2026 FRN.
  1547  1. Support for Keeping Products on the Proposed Exemption List
  1548      USTR received a number of comments expressing support for 
  1549  maintaining certain proposed exemptions. Comments supported the 
  1550  exemption of coffee, mineral tars, certain copper products, iron 
  1551  oxides, coke, aluminum oxide, and coconut products. Other comments 
  1552  expressed support for maintaining the proposed exemptions from Section 
  1553  301 tariffs for products that are subject to Section 232 tariffs. 
  1554  Commenters generally noted that these products are raw materials with 
  1555  limited-to-no availability from domestic sources or cannot be grown or 
  1556  produced in sufficient quantities or at reasonable prices in the United 
  1557  States or obtained from other sources.
  1558      Considering the public comments and the advice of the Section 301 
  1559  Committee, as well as the advice of advisory committees--and in 
  1560  accordance with the specific direction of the President--the Trade 
  1561  Representative has determined not to remove products other than the 
  1562  non-pharmaceutical applications of certain products from the proposed 
  1563  exemption list, as the remaining products in the proposed exemption 
  1564  list constitute: (1) raw materials that if subject to the proposed 
  1565  additional tariffs could lead to the unavailability of domestic supply; 
  1566  (2) products that could cause economy-wide disruptions if subject to 
  1567  the proposed additional tariffs; (3) products that cannot be grown or 
  1568  produced in sufficient quantities or at reasonable prices in the United 
  1569  States or obtained from other sources; or (4) products for which 
  1570  tariffs may not contribute substantially to the elimination of the 
  1571  acts, policies, and practices found to be actionable.
  1572  2. Determination To Remove Certain Products From the Proposed Exemption 
  1573  List
  1574      Considering the public comments and the advice of the Section 301 
  1575  Committee, as well as the advice of advisory committees--and in 
  1576  accordance with the specific direction of the President--the Trade 
  1577  Representative has determined to limit the exemption for certain 
  1578  chemicals and chemical products to their pharmaceutical applications. 
  1579  Certain comments noted the health-related applications of products 
  1580  proposed for exemptions and stated that certain ingredients that 
  1581  support U.S. manufacturing of healthcare products are not available in 
  1582  the United States in sufficient quantities to meet domestic demand. 
  1583  Some commenters also requested that these product exemptions be limited 
  1584  to their pharmaceutical applications due to competition with domestic 
  1585  production. Limiting exemptions for these proposed chemical products to 
  1586  their pharmaceutical applications is consistent with the proposal in 
  1587  the June 5, 2026 FRN because an exemption for all applications is 
  1588  broader than necessary to cover goods that have limited availability 
  1589  outside of the investigated economies.
  1590  3. Comments Requesting the Removal of Additional Products From 
  1591  Exemption List
  1592      Some commenters requested that USTR remove other products from the 
  1593  proposed exemption list or otherwise advocated for narrowly tailored 
  1594  exemptions. Industries or products for which commenters expressed
  1595  
  1596  [[Page 47331]]
  1597  
  1598  opposition to proposed exemptions include beef, avocados, paprika and 
  1599  paprika products, lithium hexafluorophosphate, and forgings and 
  1600  articles containing forgings.
  1601      Commenters suggested, for example, that beef imported from certain 
  1602  economies is linked to certain acts, policies, and practices found 
  1603  actionable in these investigations, and that exempting these products 
  1604  would benefit foreign exporters of beef produced with forced labor at 
  1605  the expense of the American cattle producer. Similarly, commenters 
  1606  suggested that paprika and paprika derived products, lithium 
  1607  hexafluorophosphate, and certain chemicals used in the production of 
  1608  pesticides are imported from certain economies linked to certain acts, 
  1609  policies, and practices found actionable in these investigations.
  1610      Additionally, commenters suggested that imports of these products 
  1611  are available from domestic sources and are putting pressure on 
  1612  domestic producers. With respect to paprika and paprika derived 
  1613  products, commenters suggested that imports have caused market 
  1614  disruptions, preventing U.S. production of these products. 
  1615  Additionally, comments reported that imports of lithium 
  1616  hexafluorophosphate and certain chemicals used in the production of 
  1617  pesticides have inhibited U.S. production of these products. Commenters 
  1618  pointed to recent and anticipated expansion in U.S. production 
  1619  capabilities, and suggested that imposing tariffs on these products 
  1620  could support investment and employment in domestic production. With 
  1621  respect to forgings and articles containing forgings, commenters 
  1622  suggested that these products are readily available from domestic 
  1623  sources, at reasonable prices, in sufficient quantities and that 
  1624  subjecting imports of these products to tariffs could support 
  1625  investment and employment in the United States. Similarly, comments 
  1626  suggested that the domestic avocado industry is under significant 
  1627  pressure due to low-priced avocado imports and applying tariffs would 
  1628  benefit certain U.S. agricultural producers.
  1629      Considering the public comments and the advice of the Section 301 
  1630  Committee, as well as the advice of advisory committees--and in 
  1631  accordance with the specific direction of the President--the Trade 
  1632  Representative has determined not to remove these products from the 
  1633  list of exempted products. There remains limited availability of these 
  1634  products from domestic sources, a point conceded by one commenter 
  1635  regarding paprika. Regarding claims that these products should be 
  1636  subject to the tariffs because they are related to acts, policies, and 
  1637  practices found actionable in these investigations, Section 
  1638  301(c)(3)(B) provides that the Trade Representative is authorized to 
  1639  take action against any goods or economic sector ``without regard to 
  1640  whether or not such goods or economic sector were involved in the act, 
  1641  policy, or practice that is the subject of such action.''
  1642  
  1643  D. Determination To Exempt Additional Products
  1644  
  1645      In addition to the products initially proposed for exemption in the 
  1646  June 5, 2026 FRN, the Trade Representative, in accordance with the 
  1647  specific direction of the President, has determined in each 
  1648  investigation to exclude an additional 471 products from tariffs 
  1649  imposed with respect to products of that economy. In certain 
  1650  investigations, the Trade Representative also has determined to apply 
  1651  additional exemptions for products from that specific investigated 
  1652  economy based on requested exemptions negotiated in the context of 
  1653  certain agreements and arrangements.
  1654      A number of comments expressed support for product exemptions in 
  1655  addition to the initial list of proposed exemptions in the June 5, 2026 
  1656  FRN. Comments requested exemptions of products including certain 
  1657  agriculture products; metals and alloys; chemicals; semiconductor 
  1658  manufacturing equipment; and art, antique, and collectible products. 
  1659  Certain economies that have concluded ARTs or similar arrangements with 
  1660  the United States have also requested exemption of products negotiated 
  1661  as part of those agreements and arrangements.
  1662      Having considered the public comments, advice of the Section 301 
  1663  Committee, as well as the advice of advisory committees, and the 
  1664  specific direction of the President, the Trade Representative 
  1665  determined to exempt the following additional products from the scope 
  1666  of actions: certain animal products; certain seeds; certain vegetable 
  1667  products; certain sugar and sugar containing products; unflavored 
  1668  instant coffee; certain fertilizer inputs and pesticide inputs; certain 
  1669  animal hides and leather; certain wood products; vanadium oxides and 
  1670  hydroxides; pig iron; certain ferrous inputs and waste; certain 
  1671  aluminum scrap waste; aluminum hydroxide; ash containing precious 
  1672  metals or precious metal compounds; certain battery waste and scrap; 
  1673  certain semiconductor manufacturing equipment; certain pharmaceuticals 
  1674  and pharmaceutical ingredients; worked shell; worn clothing; and 
  1675  certain antiques, collectibles, and art.
  1676      With respect to certain animal products used as food for animals or 
  1677  an input in such food, commenters noted that these products are 
  1678  incorporated into U.S. animal nutrition programs that support 
  1679  livestock, poultry, aquaculture, and pet food production. According to 
  1680  commenters, there is little opportunity for import substitution for 
  1681  these products and any tariff applied to these products would impose 
  1682  additional costs on U.S. consumers.
  1683      With respect to seeds of a kind used for planting, commenters noted 
  1684  that tariffs on seeds have resulted in increased costs for U.S. seed 
  1685  producers and U.S. farmers. According to comments, tariffs that impact 
  1686  seed movement erode the ability of U.S. seed companies to provide U.S. 
  1687  farmers with pure, high-quality seeds at an affordable price due to the 
  1688  global nature of seed production. Specifically, many U.S. seed 
  1689  companies have foreign operations to take advantage of environmental 
  1690  and production conditions, such as additional growing seasons. 
  1691  Commenters also noted that the increased costs associated with seed 
  1692  production could reduce choices in the marketplace for consumers as 
  1693  certain varieties of seed will no longer be viable for 
  1694  commercialization in the United States.
  1695      With respect to certain vegetable products, commenters noted that 
  1696  certain products falling under the relevant HTSUS subheading are 
  1697  already included in Annex A to the June 5, 2026 FRN, but that the 
  1698  proposed product exemptions are limited to products used for religious 
  1699  purposes only. According to comments, products in the relevant HTSUS 
  1700  subheading are essential growing-media and fiber inputs used in nursery 
  1701  production that have no domestic source, including coconut coir, jute 
  1702  burlap, and sisal twine. According to comments, the crops used to 
  1703  produce these products are not commercially grown in the United States 
  1704  given climate limitations and, therefore, there is no domestic industry 
  1705  capable of producing these inputs for the U.S. horticulture sector.
  1706      With respect to in-quota imports of certain sugar and sugar-
  1707  containing products, commenters noted that U.S. sugar producers are 
  1708  more efficient than ever and domestic sugar yields have increased, yet 
  1709  the United States has never produced enough sugar to meet its domestic 
  1710  demand. To meet this demand, the United States has historically had to 
  1711  import significant amounts of sugar. According to comments, U.S. sugar 
  1712  processing
  1713  
  1714  [[Page 47332]]
  1715  
  1716  facilities rely on certain in-quota sugar to meet U.S. demand and 
  1717  supply a critical input of the U.S. food supply chain.
  1718      With respect to unflavored instant coffee, commenters noted that

Q2.answer: (a) Customs value $40,000 each. Entry 1, Aug. 20, 2026, 2:00 p.m.: $0. Entry 2, Aug. 21, 11:59 p.m.: $0. Entry 3, Aug. 22, 12:01 a.m.: 50% x $40,000 = $20,000. Controlling text: Proclamation 11056 clause (1), FR Doc. 2026-17294, 91 FR 54790, effective date of duties in Proclamations 11046-11048 shall be Aug. 22, 2026, 12:01 a.m. ET, measured against entered/withdrawn goods under original clauses (1)/(3). (b) Original Proclamation 11046 clauses (1) and (3), 91 FR 46641, print Aug. 19, 2026, 12:01 a.m. ET, entered/withdrawn. Proclamation 11056 clause (1) amends only the chapeau of Annex II of each original proclamation, deleting Aug. 19 and inserting Aug. 22; it does not textually amend clauses (1)/(3) of 11046-11048. The later operative effective date (Aug. 22) in the suspension proclamation, confirmed by Proclamation 11061 para. 4, 91 FR 58311, and 11064 para. 4, 91 FR 58331 (suspension lapsed, duties became effective Aug. 22), resolves the difference in favor of Aug. 22. (c) Proclamation 11056 clause (4), 91 FR 54791: to extent implementation requires refund of duties collected, refunds shall be processed pursuant to applicable law and CBP standard procedures. Clause (2) directs suspension of collection to extent required. No other refund mechanism is stated in readable text. (d) No further presidential action was needed to begin: original duties were self-effective on the stated date, HTSUS modified by Annex II, clause (3), 91 FR 46641. Later documents state the 3-day suspension lapsed Aug. 22 and duties became effective automatically, Proclamation 11061 para. 4, 91 FR 58311; Proclamation 11064 para. 4, 91 FR 58331. They also state Canada reneged Aug. 21 and ceased negotiating in good faith, 11061 para. 3, 91 FR 58311. (e) Section 338 text, Proclamation 11046 para. 10, 91 FR 46640: duties not to exceed 50% and not to take effect earlier than 30 days after the President's proclamation finding discrimination. Arithmetic: Proclamation 11046 of July 20, 2026, finding in paras. 7-9, 91 FR 46640; July 20 + 30 days = Aug. 19, 2026 (July 20 to Aug. 19 = 30 days), the original date printed in para. 9 and clauses (1)/(3), 91 FR 46640-46641. Rate: 50% is the stated maximum in para. 10 and the rate imposed in para. 9 / clause (1).
Q2.uncertainty: Annex II chapeau is an unreadable image; its amendment is taken from clause (1) text of Proclamation 11056.

Q3.answer: Value $30,000, MFN free, 50% duty = 50% x $30,000 = $15,000 if dutiable and importable. (a)(A) Arrives Sept. 10, entered Sept. 14: imported before Sept. 29, 2026, so not banned; entered before Sept. 29, duty applies. May be imported, section 338 duty $15,000. (B) Arrives Sept. 27, bonded warehouse, withdrawn Oct. 5: imported before Sept. 29, clause (2) of Proclamation 11061, 91 FR 58312, imported but not yet withdrawn before Sept. 29 remains subject to 50% duty. May be imported, duty $15,000 on withdrawal. (C) Arrives Sept. 28, 11:30 p.m., entry filed Sept. 29, 9:00 a.m.: imported before Sept. 29, 12:01 a.m. ET, so clause (2) applies despite entry after Sept. 29. May be imported, duty $15,000. (D) Arrives Sept. 29, 12:30 a.m., entry that morning: imported on/after Sept. 29, 12:01 a.m. ET, clause (1), 91 FR 58312, excluded from importation. May not be imported; no lawful entry duty assessed. (b) Shipment E arrives Sept. 25, admitted to FTZ Sept. 25, entry Oct. 6: imported before Sept. 29, so not banned; FTZ admission after original effective date Aug. 22 must be privileged foreign status under original clause (4), 91 FR 46641, but that does not remove duty. Subject to 50% duty on entry Oct. 6: on $30,000, $15,000. (c) If import exclusion invalid as applied: Proclamation 11061 clause (9)(b), 91 FR 58313, 50% duty in Proclamation 11046 shall apply to import to which invalidated ban had applied before invalidation. Shipments imported after ruling may be imported and bear 50% duty, $15,000 per $30,000 shipment. (d) No. Exclusion clause (3), 91 FR 58312: besides changing Annex products to ban, proclamation does not otherwise affect products as further established in Sept. 8 alcoholic-beverage scope proclamation that are subject to 11046 duties. Non-Annex listed products remain subject to 50% duty as modified by scope proclamation.

(d) Equivalent-rate rule is stated in U.S. Note 52(k), Annex I to Notice 2026-15181, 91 FR 47394: for EU, Japan, South Korea, Switzerland, Taiwan goods subject to specific/compound column 1-General, equivalent = duty payable divided by customs value, with example. Result at/above cap is stated in same Note 52(k) final sentences, 91 FR 47394 (below cap sums to 10% or 12.5%), and in Memorandum Sec. 1(a)(ii), 91 FR 47720, and specific determinations, e.g. EU/Taiwan at/above 10% section 301 zero, Japan/Korea/Switzerland at/above 12.5% zero, 91 FR 47323, 47327.
Q7.basis: Notice 2026-15181 Note 52(k), 91 FR 47394; Memorandum Sec. 1(a)(ii), 91 FR 47720; determinations EU, Japan, Switzerland, Taiwan, 91 FR 47323-47328.

Q8.answer: Dominican Republic flat 12.5%, $80,000 x 12.5% = $10,000 if dutiable, MFN free. (a) 1. Q10.answer: Scenario 1, $200,000, MFN 3%: (a) Sept. 10, 2026 - MFN: 3% x $200,000 = $6,000; section 232: 50% x $200,000 = $100,000, entered under 9903.82.02; section 338: $0, original motor-vehicle clause (2) provides duties shall not apply to articles subject to section 232, 91 FR 46665, and Sept. scope not yet effective; section 301: $0, Canada 10% rate but U.S. Note 52(f)(1) exempts aluminum articles in 9903.82.02 from section 301, 91 FR 47362. Total of all layers = $106,000. (b) Sept. 16, 2026 - MFN $6,000; section 232 $100,000; section 338: 50% x $200,000 = $100,000, because Sept. scope clause (1) effective Sept. 15, 2026, 12:01 a.m. ET, provides duties as modified shall apply in addition to section 232, 91 FR 58340, superseding the prior exclusion by clause (7); section 301 $0 as in (a). Total = $206,000. Scenario 2, $60,000, MFN free: (c) Sept. 1, 2026, USMCA free entry - section 338: 50% x $60,000 = $30,000; goods imported before Sept. 29 remain subject to 50% duty under exclusion clause (2), 91 FR 58312, and no readable USMCA exemption from section 338 applies; section 301: $0, Note 52(g) exempts products of Canada entered free under USMCA from heading 9903.05.29, 91 FR 47363. Total asked = $30,000. (d) Sept. 1, 2026, no USMCA claim - section 338 $30,000 as in (c); section 301: Canada 10% x $60,000 = $6,000, Memorandum Sec. 1(a)(i), 91 FR 47720, and Notice determination 10, 91 FR 47322. Total = $36,000. (e) Arrival Oct. 2, 2026 - imported on/after Sept. 29, 2026, 12:01 a.m. ET, so excluded from importation under Proclamation 11061 clause (1), 91 FR 58312; it may not be lawfully imported/entered, so no section 338 or section 301 duty is payable on a lawful entry. If it were entered, the duty figures in (d) would be the arithmetic, but the exclusion bars importation. (f) IEEPA northern-border duties: imposed by EO 14193, FR Doc. 2025-02406, 90 FR 9113, 25% from Feb. 4, 2025, as paused to Mar. 4, 2025 by EO 14197, FR Doc. 2025-02478, 90 FR 9183, USMCA exemption from Mar. 7, 2025 by EO 14231, FR Doc. 2025-03990, 90 FR 11785, increased to 35% Aug. 1, 2025 by EO 14325, FR Doc. 2025-14999, 90 FR 37957, and ended by EO 14389, FR Doc. 2026-03832, 91 FR 9437, signed Feb. 20, 2026, published Feb. 25, 2026, Sec. 1: IEEPA duties in EO 14193 shall no longer be in effect/collected. 10% temporary surcharge: Proclamation 11012, FR Doc. 2026-03824, 91 FR 9339, signed Feb. 20, 2026, published Feb. 25, 2026, clause (7), 91 FR 9342-9343: effective Feb. 24, 2026 through 12:01 a.m. EDT July 24, 2026, entered/withdrawn. Therefore neither duty applies to Canadian goods entered in September 2026.
